utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Before we begin today, there are a couple the matters the Chamber would like to deal with. First the Chamber will issue an oral ruling on the "Prosecution application regarding the report on use of time in the trial" filed on 4th of April, 2012. In the application -- very familiar sound. In the application, the Prosecution requests the Trial Chamber to direct the Registry to provide a breakdown of the time calculations for each witness who testified during -- between the 1st and the 29th of March, 2012, and requests to be allowed to file an application challenging the time used by it within seven days from the receipt of the breakdown of the time calculations. The Chamber hereby grants both requests and orders the Registry to provide the time statistics for March to the Prosecution as soon as practicable and orders the Prosecution to file its challenge within seven days of the receipt of these time statistics. Next, on the 23rd of March, 2012, the accused filed the "Motion to modify protective measures: Witness KDZ071," requesting the rescission of the protective measures granted to Witness KDZ071 in the Krstic case. On the 28th of March, 2012, the Prosecution filed its response opposing the motion and referring to the witness's conversation of 27th of March, 2012, with the Prosecution's investigator during the course of which he stated that he needed his protective measures to be continued as he has returned to the Srebrenica area and feels unsafe. The Chamber first notes that there is no Chamber currently seized of the Krstic case within the meaning of Rule 75(G) and that none of the Judges who granted the original protective measures to the witness in the Krstic case remain at the Tribunal. On the 5th of April, 2012, the Chamber was informed by the VWS pursuant to Rule 75(J) that the witness does not consent to the rescission of his protective measures. The Chamber also recalls that under Rule 75(J) of the Rules, it may order the rescission of protective measures absent the consent of the witness in exceptional circumstances and "on the basis of a compelling showing of the exigent circumstances or where a miscarriage of justice would otherwise result." The Chamber has carefully examined the motion and its annex therein and considers that exceptional circumstances that would warrant the rescission of the protective measures absent the consent of the witness have not been shown. The Chamber therefore dismisses the accused's motion, and accordingly, Witness KDZ071 shall testify with the protective measures of pseudonym and image distortion. The Chamber has noted the witness's statement that he has not made any public declaration since returning to the Srebrenica area. However, the Chamber would like to remind the witness that any public statement he makes will render his protective measures ineffective and therefore warns him against doing so. That said, we'll -- back to normal proceedings. If the witness take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I apologise for your inconvenience, and please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Amor Masovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You've testified before the Tribunal in four cases and you have provided statements to representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Recently a statement was taken from you which amalgamated evidence from your previous testimonies and statements, and you also provided clarifications and some additional comments in relation to a number of documents; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter number 90326 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON

utterances.text: We'll admit both versions. Shall we give the numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the public version will become Exhibit P4850, and the confidential P4851, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: With Your Honours' leave, I will now read a brief summary of the witness's evidence. The witness is a member of the board of directors of the Missing Persons Institute of Bosnia and Herzegovina commonly known as the MPI. The MPI's responsibilities include maintaining lists of missing persons and persons who have been found through the process of exhumation and identification. The MPI, which began functioning in January 2008, assumed the responsibilities of the commissions for missing persons that had been in existence in Bosnia-Herzegovina prior to that time. During 1992 to 1995, the witness was a member, acting head and deputy head of the BiH State Commission for Exchange of Prisoners of War Captured Persons and Bodies of People Killed and Record of People Killed, Injured and Missing on the Territory of the Republic of BiH, known as the State Commission. In 1996, the State Commission became the State Commission for Tracing Missing Persons. The witness was appointed president of this commission. As of July 1997, the witness was also appointed as chairman and co-chairman of the Federal Commission for Tracing Missing Persons that encompassed the State Commission and a commission established by the Bosnian Croat authorities. The witness's evidence relates to the work of these institutions, their mandate, their methodology, and their findings. The witness gives details of his duties and responsibilities in these institutions including his participation in the process of exhumations, autopsies and identification of victims exhumed from mass graves, common graves, and individual graves throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina. The witness reviewed and commented upon several documents relating to exchanges during the war and a number of documents relating to exhumations, autopsies and identifications conducted in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The witness has prepared a report on exhumed and identified persons relating to the incidents listed in Schedules A and B to the indictment in this case from the MPI records. That completes the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, I have a small number of questions for you. In your amalgamated statement, you discuss the process of exhumation, autopsies, and identification of victims, and you say that the institute maintains lists of exhumed and identified victims as well as missing persons. In October 2009, did you provide a report to the OTP on exhumed and identified persons based on these MPI records in relation to persons listed in Schedules A and B to the indictment?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And does that report contain two tables, the first table containing numerical data on the number of persons exhumed and identified or missing from several municipalities, and the second table contains data about individual victims that have been exhumed and identified?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter number 23691 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is this your report that you provided in October 2009?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And attached to that report were the two tables, Table 1 and Table 2 that we've just discussed?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And this report sets out the methodology and quotes a number of figures that were -- that were correct as at the time of writing the report?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And did the OTP then recently ask you to update the information contained in the two tables?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND

utterances.text: Now, we see on the left-hand side the -- is that the report, the updated report that -- if we could just scroll over a little bit so we can see the date in the heading of the document.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the updated list as of the 5th of April, 2012.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And on the right-hand side of the screen we can see an English translation of the heading row, the title of the document, the heading row and also the legend which we will now go to, because I want you to explain the colours that we can see in the document. If we could go to the last page of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: In essence, the legend refers to two types of exhumed persons and identified. The first group are persons whose names were provided to me by the OTP. These are persons who are marked in red and blue text in the table. The difference between those marked in red and in blue is in the updating. Persons marked in red are persons who were identified at the time of the drafting of the first report in 2009, and persons whose names are written in blue are persons who were subsequently identified in the period since 2009 until the drafting of the new report in April 2012. The second part of the legend or the text that is written in black refers to persons who were exhumed and identified and are not found on the lists of victims that were provided to me by the OTP. However, these are persons who were found in the same mass graves in which the persons whose names were provided to me by the OTP were found, whose names are in red and blue ink. They were included in the list based on the fact that they were found, exhumed, and identified in the same mass graves as those persons whose names were provided to me by the OTP. The difference between the persons in black and those in black with a blue star is in the updating. Again, the lists were updated. Those whose names are written only in black were identified at the time the first report was drafted in 2009, and those whose names are written in black with a blue star next to their names are persons who were identified in the period since 2009 until April 2012.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And just looking at this last page of the document, we can see five victims in relation to Foca, and if we could just zoom out so that we can see all of the page. We can see four names in red provided by the OTP and then one name in black coming --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we collapse the English translation for the moment, yes, and zoom in in B/C/S. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, we can see the six [sic] names in red and the one name in black, all being exhumed from the same mass grave.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct. All five persons were exhumed on the 17th of December, 2008, in Usce Cehotina, that location which is a mass grave in the Foca municipality area, and the name of four of the identified persons are on the OTP victim's list that was provided to me, whereas the fifth person, Kemal Isanovic, marked in black, is not on the OTP victim list. He was included in this list on the basis of criteria I referred to before and that is the fact that he was found in the same mass grave.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, just looking there we can see a column "Date of disappearance" and where the person was last seen; is that right? Can you just explain to the Trial Chamber how the date and place missing columns were determined.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: The sources that were used by the entity commissions and, before them, by the State Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners of War and the State Commission for Missing Persons are different information. The most frequent sources of information about the missing persons, the date they went missing, the place of missing and the circumstances were the actual families of those persons, but not necessarily so. In situations of missing members of armies or missing members from the police force and so on and so forth, in that case information about the missing persons were provided by their commands, authorised services, their superiors, and even their co-fighters who were witnesses when they went missing. If you look at the dates reported as the dates the person went missing, very often it can be the case that this is not the actual date of death of a missing person. It's simply a date that one of our sources of information acquired. For example, in certain cases a member of the family who survived the war was a witness when his close relative was taken away from his apartment, from their house, from their property or simply from the street, and that was the last day that that person saw their relative alive, and he would report that day as the day the person went missing. However, in many cases, such missing persons, after being taken away from their homes, were taken to camps, prisons, and in such cases some other prisoners or detainees would see that person even months after the person was taken away from their apartment or their house, and then they would testify to a different date and a different place of -- the person went missing and different circumstances. My conclusion, therefore, is that the date and the place the person went missing does not have to indicate the actual date that a person went missing. It's more of a perceived date by a member of the family, and even different members of the same family could provide different information about the date a person went missing depending on when each of them learned that their relative had gone missing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, you referred to the column "Date of disappearance" and the column where the person was last seen, but I can't find those two columns in the English translation. Where do we have it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's -- if we can ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let us collapse the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's the sixth and seventh column, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And can we see the B/C/S now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So, Mr. Masovic, can you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Now I can find them. Thank you, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So, Mr. Masovic, if I understand you well, when you had different dates from the family and then a subsequent date of the person being seen at another location, you made the assessment to put the later date as the date of disappearance; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Not necessarily. We try to check the veracity of the date -- or, rather, the credibility of the resource that provided it. So based on how credible the source is, we would enter such data. I have to underline that for our institution, both the former district commission and the institute of today, all the circumstances and information surrounding the disappearance are not significant data. Our task was not to find out how the people went missing and who was responsible. Our major task was to try and locate the missing person, and unfortunately most of them were found to be dead after the war. Another task of ours was to identify those persons and to hand over their remains to their families. That was our main concern. As for the dates and manner of disappearance are something that the Bosnian prosecutor offices and regular courts are dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could just go to page 11 of the document in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, you can see in front of you this page relates to the mass grave at Laniste 1 dealing with victims from Biljani. Very briefly, the same principle as you've just discussed applies in relation to the red and the black names; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Before I answer, there is a mistake in the English version, but now it's been corrected. Yes. The red names indicate the victims that are on the OTP list. The black names are not on the OTP list. However, they were found in the same mass grave which was in the area of Laniste, near Kljuc, and which was 20 metres deep. So the remains of all these victims were found in this one and the same grave, and its official name was Laniste 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, I want to ask you about the entries that you have for Bijeljina. If we could go to page 1 of the document. Can you explain to the Court why Bijeljina appears to be different from the rest of the table? We see here that there's four names in red exhumed from individual graves at one location and a number of other persons whose names appear in black text again exhumed from individual graves but from another location. Why did you list these names in black?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: The names of these individuals are written in black because their names are not on the OTP list that was made available to me which contains 48 names of the victims. Of the 48, only first four individuals that we see in this table marked in red are in the OTP list, whereas the rest are not. They were put on the Bijeljina list because this involves the persons that for many years had been considered as missing, and they went missing in the area of Bijeljina. Some of them disappeared until the first half of April 1992, and some of them went missing towards the end of 1992, with the exception of the Kisic family, six-member family --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, Isic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- which is the family that disappeared in Bijeljina in 1993. Therefore, all of them, with exception of one person that was found in the same grave as the first four victims, the Komsic family, were found in Serbia. Komsic family was found in a cemetery in Bijeljina, whereas the others were found in Serbia. I suppose that these people had been first killed, then their bodies were dumped into the Drina River, and from then on their bodies were taken down the Sava River to Serbia where the local authorities took these bodies out and buried them in Sremska Mitrovica, Sabac and Belgrade, and they were buried as unidentified persons until the date when their identity was established through DNA examination. The 12 people whose names are marked in black were reported as missing either in the beginning or by mid-April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender that -- I seek to tender the report, which was 65 ter number 23690, and the updated table, this updated Table 2 which is 23691B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The original report, the number of original report should be 23691.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry. Yes, Your Honour. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We don't have any objection to 23691B, but we do object to 23690, since this is not an expert witness. Any information in his report should have actually been included and probably is included to some degree in the amalgamated statement pursuant to the Chamber's practice. Secondly, I note that the Prosecution has provided us by e-mail with an updated list of the other table that was contained in the report and I think that that should be admitted but not the narrative of the report. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you expand on the reasons why the previous report, part of which is already incorporated into his update, should be excluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We believe that the tables only should be admitted, so that for 619B only the table that we've been discussion should be admitted, and we also request that the other table be admitted which is an update to the other table that was contained in 23691. However, the narrative itself we don't believe should be admitted because this witness is not an expert for whose report has been noticed and that's normally admitted as an expert report. He's a fact witness, and you've indicated that for fact witnesses their information should be amalgamated into a single statement and that that single statement should be admitted, which you've already admitted his statement. So we don't believe that the narrative of the report should be admitted into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So it is your submission that the narrative part of this report, i.e., 23691, amounts to an expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I'm saying that it has no business being admitted because it's not an expert witness. So even if it's not an expert report, whatever information that the Prosecution wanted to tender outside of the oral testimony should have been included in the amalgamated statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Can I hear from you, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, as you know, this is a fact witness with expertise. He may not be an expert witness, but he is a fact witness who has expertise. The narrative to the report simply sets out the criteria he used in putting data in Table 1 and Table 2 and his methodology for doing that. He does elucidate on that in paragraphs in his amalgamated statement, but it's our submission that this overview would help even though the figures that are contained in -- in the report may not be current at the moment in the narrative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Both will be admitted given that Defence has no objection to the admission of the table and that the witness -- witness's narrative helps the Chamber understand the methodology in preparing for those tables. The objection is overruled, and we admit them. We'll give the numbers to both versions.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit P4852 and P4853. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There's no problem in admitting publicly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Table 2, no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the report, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, I want to turn now to the other table in the report, Table 1. You were also asked to update that table, were you not?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could 65 ter number 23691A on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct. This is Table 1 that also contains updated information about the missing persons that had been located and identified in a number of municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And briefly what is the difference between this updated table and the original table in 2009?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: The principal difference is in that in the updated 2012 table, two municipalities, i.e., Visegrad and Kotor Varos, were left out. I suppose that they have also been left out from the indictment. As for the other municipalities, the data have been altered in term of establishing new numbers of the missing persons and identified persons. Some persons were found in the period between 2009 and 2012. Some of them found in that period were identified, including some that were found prior to 2009 but were only identified later.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we could go to the second page. And the last -- and then the last page. I tender that updated Table 1, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Robinson, separate from the issues that you raised, I forgot to ask you whether you were happy with the extent or degree of English translation of those document.

utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, I wish to now turn to the victim list. Were you recently requested by the Office of the Prosecutor to review its corrected victim list?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Do we need to have it on our screens first?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, my question was simply were you asked to review a corrected version of the witness list that was provided by the -- victim list which was provided by the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter number 23690A on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, is this the updated victim list that you provided to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. It is an updated list of victims as indicated in the title of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, can you explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could the Chamber move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So very, very quickly, Mr. Masovic, can you just explain what's on the right-hand -- left-hand side of the screen.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I only have one list on my screen, which is the list provided to me by the OTP. So on the left-hand side is the list of the alleged victims provided by the OTP for the purpose of me reviewing the list and giving my comment. On the right-hand side of the screen you can see which comment I made with respect to each of the victims on the left-hand side or on the so-called OTP victims list.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the -- the columns that you added are shaded in grey in the heading column. Now, can you just briefly explain for the Trial Chamber the different categories that are represented there. If we could go to the last page, we see a legend, but I would like you to very briefly explain to the Chamber the different colours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can go to the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, this involves the persons that were on the OTP victims list. When I made my comments, I used light yellow to mark all those victims who were identified to date. Light green indicates the names of the victims that have not yet been found, or if they have been found, they haven't been identified yet, which their status remains as still missing. Colour brown indicates the victims from the OTP list which still have formally the status of missing persons, but we do have some kind of preliminary identity for these persons established on the basis of DNA identification. So it is highly likely, and let me say that I estimate it to be 95 [as interpreted] per cent possibility that in the course of further identification that is going to be carried out with the assistance of their families, these victims will be transferred to the category marked in light yellow, which means those who have been definitely identified. And finally, we have the category that is not coloured by any colour, which is white, and that refers to the alleged victims from the OTP list that had not been reported at all as missing to the institute of Bosnia-Herzegovina or in which cases the information we received was inaccurate or insufficient and therefore unable to assist me in establishing their identity. For example, if only you have the last name of the victim without his or her first name or his or her father's name, this is not enough, because it is well known that dozens or hundreds of families or members of one and the same family were killed. But if I only have the last name of the family without any other details, I really find it difficult to determine which particular member of that family was involved. For that reason, we left this category blank pending the final determination of the status of these persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, the transcript reads that you said that you estimated it to be 95 per cent possibility that the preliminary identifications --

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, I wish to turn briefly to another topic. In your work in the institute, have you ever come across situations of persons falsely claiming military benefits and for what reason?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: It is difficult to answer this question. We in the institute are actually not involved in keeping these kinds of records. In my report, I did mention some attempts, but it didn't have to do with any particular military records, but nevertheless I said that there were attempts by some members of the families to obtain some benefits. Over the 20 years that I have been working with missing persons, in only three instances we realised that families tried to report their family members missing in order to obtain some kind of remuneration. So from the date when I started working until today, there were only three such attempt -- attempts. As far as your question is concerned, I can say that I am aware of such instances but not within the scope of work that I am involved in. According to the electronic and other media, apparently there were quite a few cases in which certain individuals succeeded in acquiring certain statuses in spite of the fact that they were not eligible for that. For example, they reported some of their family members as being killed and claimed them to have been members of the military, which in fact is something that they were not entitled to, and I think that this is prevailing in both entities. And I think that in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina there are efforts which have been lasting for quite some time to establish precisely who was the member of the military or other formations, because as you know, Bosnia is facing an economic crisis just like the rest of the world, and I think that these economic difficulties have accelerated the process of reviewing the requests for these remunerations.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I just make one intervention in the transcript, because I don't think I'll be able to do that during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well, yes. But please wait, because you overlapped, but, yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think at page 22, 11, 12, and 13, the witness said not a small number of such cases, but here it says quite a few cases. So lines 11, 12, and 13 on page 22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That will -- that's noted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I can't find that in the transcript. If you could go back a bit. I don't know what it relates to. I said two things. I said there was one situation which only three attempts were recorded, three attempts to report that someone had allegedly gone missing, but there was no one who had gone missing. And then I mentioned something that wasn't part of the responsibilities of the Institute for Missing Persons, something I was aware of given what I had read in the press or through the electronic media. I heard that there was a review underway and that it appeared that there were -- there wasn't a small number of cases in which certain individuals obtained financial compensation or certain benefits although they were not entitled to such benefits. To be more precise, some individuals were granted the status of members of the military, of the police force, whereas in fact those individuals were never members of the military or of the police force. Or some individuals were granted were granted a certain status as disabled individuals and as a result they had financial compensation, but these people in fact weren't disabled or they didn't have disability of such a percentage that would have resulted in that individual obtaining financial compensation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Masovic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Sutherland. Shall we deal with the associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We have objections to several of the associated exhibits which contain the reports of autopsies, and our objection is that to admit those through this witness would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you let us know the number of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, number first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: 13081, 12602 [Realtime transcript read in error "12601"], 13106. 12918, we actually object to that document as not forming an indispensable part of the statement. Then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. 12601. Is it included in the associated exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think I said 12062.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 12062. And the last one is 12 ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: And then also 13064, 13024, 13061, 13093, and 04786. And there were also a number of documents which didn't have English translations, so we weren't able to be sure whether they included autopsy reports or were simply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I will come back to the documents where English translations are missing, but -- so please proceed with your first issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, with respect to this issue, I think that we've already encountered this when we dealt with the testimony of Dean Manning, when the Prosecution sought to incorporate into its exhibits the reports of -- or findings of other experts who were not testifying or no notice of their expert reports were submitted to us under 94 bis and you ruled that those would not be admitted, and we think that this presents the same issue and ought to end in the same result, which is that those exhibits dealing with expert autopsy reports ought not to be admitted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Because I didn't have time to go through each and every document, I note that, for example, 4786, the last item you referred to, has an English translation. So by way of an example, could you give us an example why certain parts should not be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could we upload that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: If we look starting at page 5 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. If we could just look starting at page 5, which is -- we are objecting in this document to pages 5 through 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So forensic medical examination and postmortem examination of the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct. And for each of the bodies the expert gives his opinion as to the cause of death, and so we think that that ought to be something that should have been the subject of expert testimony and shouldn't be admitted through this witness. He himself on occasion has been present. He has observed some bodies and remains and has given his opinion of what he found in the comments section to the annex, but with respect to actual autopsy reports and results, we don't believe that they should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Your Honour, Mr. Tieger --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'd like to hear one at a time. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger is going to deal with this issue. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. This is a misleading and false analogy both in terms of the jurisprudence cited during the course of the argument with regard to the Manning materials and with regard to those materials themselves extending to this issue. Let me explain as briefly as I can. First of all, during the course of the argument on the Manning materials, Mr. Robinson relied on two things, the decision regarding investigator Barney Kelly's summaries in the Milosevic case in May of 2002, which was finally decided by the Appeals Chamber in September of 2002, and he relied on 94 bis as lex specialis. With respect to the Kelly decision, that decision turned on the fact that the summaries were done by an OTP employee. That is not the case here. In fact, contrary to Mr. Robinson's assertion, the -- both the Trial Chamber in Milosevic and the Appeals Chamber in rendering its decision specifically and explicitly approved of summaries and the submission of such materials through other witnesses when they weren't done by OTP employees, and they cited specifically the human rights -- the testimony of Fred Abrahams who incorporated previous statements and an OSCE report and other documents by extension. By analogy, that would mean that in this particular case these reports would come in. Finally, the decision in the Milosevic case was grounded upon the finding by the Trial Chamber that there was little or no probative value in the tendered materials. That is precisely the opposite of the situation here. Here the Trial Chamber, this Trial Chamber, in its decision of February 21st, 2012, explicitly found that these materials have probative value and are relevant but simply asked that they be tendered through a witness. Secondly with respect to 94 bis, Mr. Robinson attempts to make -- extend it beyond the practice of this jurisprudence and indeed beyond the explicit provisions of 94 bis which is not a provision which embraces every single document which has any specialised or expertise component, it addresses specifically the testimony of expert witness, that's the title of 94 bis, and it refers to the statements or reports of an expert witness to be called by a party. It was never intended to embrace every single document that might have been produced at any time during the course of the conflict or thereafter with respect to relevant issues. It was related specifically to this. That is -- it has never been the practice in this institution to make outside autopsy reports or exhumation reports the subject of 94 bis, and I've canvassed the case in other cases. That hasn't been the case. Exhumation reports and autopsies have been submitted in various ways but not under 94 bis. It's not the practice in this case where we have seen autopsy reports and exhumations submitted through witnesses who did not conduct them and not under 94 bis. The Defence knows that because they tendered two autopsy reports through different witnesses themselves not under 94 bis already in this case. And we know it's not the case because this Trial Chamber itself made a decision on February 21st, 2012, when it reviewed the tendering of exhumation reports through bar table and -- and determined that, again as I mentioned, that they were probative and relevant but should be tendered through a witness but again made no mention whatsoever of 94 bis, confirming the practice in this institution and in this particular case that these are not -- reports such as these do not fall under 94 bis. And finally with respect directly to the Manning analogy, that decision by the Trial Chamber here involved reports that the OTP had asked certain experts to produce. That's completely different from the situation we have here where these were reports that were not commissioned by the OTP but that were produced in the course of business by outside agencies. So the bottom line, Mr. President, is this: The OTP has done precisely what the Trial Chamber asked it to do on February 21st, and that was to tender these documents through a witness. That's not only completely consistent with the jurisprudence of this institution but actually goes an extra mile by the Trial Chamber in doing so. And I would say this witness who oversaw much of this process and indeed in a very hands-on way is the perfect witness through whom to do so. Even if he wasn't the perfect witness, that would only go to weight not to admissibility. I could also speak for quite a long time about the policies and practices underpinning the general nature of admissibility in this institution, but given the specific backdrop of this issue, I don't think that's necessary unless the Trial Chamber does. These documents should be admitted as they have been tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could kindly remind us what the -- our decision of 21st of February involved. Was it not related to exhumation report, not including the forensic postmortem examination that would touch upon the cause of death?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, that is true, Mr. President, but I cited it for the broad principle that such matters do not involve 94 bis. I think it clearly stands for that proposition. I cited it also for the proposition that the trial -- that the Prosecution has acted as directed to by the -- by the Chamber, and I continue to note that autopsy reports have been admitted in this case through witness -- through means other than 94 bis, through witnesses who did not conduct the autopsies, and that that is a practice that is not only followed in this Trial Chamber but based on my canvassing of all the available information has been the consistent practice in this institution throughout for the reasons I described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And one further reason for the Chamber to have denied that -- denied to admit those exhumation report through bar table motion was to give the accused an opportunity to cross-examine as to its content. So how can we compromise with that ruling in this case, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It is not a compromise on that ruling, Mr. President, I would submit. First of all, the decision said it should be tendered through a witness who can comment on the -- I should find the exact language but who can speak to them and answer questions in relation thereto. This witness is clearly in a position to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The next sentence. This would also give the accused the opportunity to cross-examine such a witness and test his or her evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. This witness can talk about the circumstances that gave rise to these examinations, the nature of the process that was pursued, its consistency with all the other information that was available, the persons who were tasked to conduct these -- these matters. The fact of the matter is that that -- it's not -- and I'm going to say it again, we have admitted autopsy reports before in a matter that's completely consistent with the most stringent adversarial system jurisdictions. That is, where people have come in and said yes, that was done, this is not an autopsy report done by some third grader, this is a matter done in the normal course of business as one would expect. That's part of what this witness can testify to and he can testify to much more giving the Court a contextualised understanding of how these things arose, the fact that they were conducted by professionals for a particular reason in -- in the course of an effort that was independent of an OTP commissioning akin to the Manning reports or to the Kelly reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I was waiting for the completion of French translation. Mr. Masovic, the Chamber does not usually hear from the witness during the course of debate, so if you could wait for the moment. Yes, Mr. Robinson. Would you like to say anything further?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, just briefly in reply. I think the Chamber has hit the nail on the head which is who is Dr. Karadzic going to cross-examine about the cause of death if these reports are admitted through this witness, and that was the basis for your ruling with respect to the Dean Manning issue for which the Prosecution didn't seek reconsideration, and I think that should be the basis for your ruling here. The last time I heard Mr. Tieger relying on the practice of this institution was when he tried to justify not disclosing Rule 68 material before the beginning of the trial, and you've ruled that that practice was wrong, and it would be wrong to also allow the Prosecution to have the benefit of expert evidence without following the procedure under Rule 94 bis which provides for notice in advance of the trial, provides for the opportunity for the accused to either agree or dispute the expert evidence, and then where it's disputed, it gives the accused the opportunity to cross-examine expert witnesses. And so we believe that that practice should require that if the Prosecution wants to rely on expert evidence outside of court, it should have followed that procedure and given the Defence the opportunity to challenge it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just could confirm that -- that the part the Defence is concerned about is the part related to the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I can't sit while Mr. Robinson asserts that I am trying to disregard the rules of the institution. 94 bis does not provide for and is not intended to encompass the documents that he is seeking to bar from admission, and it doesn't -- it doesn't embrace those documents on its face, it hasn't embraced those documents in the course of the practice of this institution, and it hasn't embraced those documents in the course of the practice in this case as reflected by the fact that the Defence itself tendered such documents, and those were, for example, D48 and D2043 through two separate witnesses. And I mentioned the other aspects of the adversarial system because it would be anomalous to the point of being bizarre if this institution, which has adopted an expansive admissibility policy in light of the scale of the events and the scope of evidence that is admitted which can be tested one against the other, to have a practice that is more constrictive and restrictive than adversarial systems which would allow such documents to be admitted when they are produced in -- in the customary course of business of those institutions. So for many reasons this is not a matter of the OTP trying to circumvent the rules of the institution. This is instead a reflection of Mr. Robinson's attempt to expand a rule beyond the scope of what it is intended for and what it has been applied to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber will rise for its deliberation. So we'll probably resume at 11.00, but Mr. Tieger, Mr. Robinson, Mr. Karadzic, due to my personal urgent matters, I will be absent from the remainder of this week, and the Chamber will sit pursuant to Rule 15 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: The Chamber has considered the arguments put forth by the parties in relation to the admission of the autopsy reports. The Chamber recalls that the rationale behind its decision of the 21st of February, 2012, was to provide the accused with an opportunity to cross-examine a witness who can answer questions as to the parts of the exhumation reports that he challenges. The accused indicated today that he challenged the causes of death in these reports. The Chamber therefore considers that it is not appropriate to admit these parts of the autopsy reports dealing with the causes of death but sees no reason not to admit the rest of these documents. The Chamber therefore orders that the Prosecution provide redacted versions of 65 ter 4786, 12602, 12918, 13024, 13061, 13064, 13081, 13093, and 13106, and will admit these redacted versions into evidence. The Chamber has also noted that a number of English translations are missing. For those documents for which no English translations have been provided, the Chamber will MFI the documents pending reception of the English translation. The Chamber will admit the remainder of the associated exhibits into evidence and ask the Registry to attribute the appropriate exhibit number in due course. Thank you. Now, are there any more matters to be dealt with by the Prosecution in relation to this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: So be it. Mr. Witness, the accused now has the opportunity to cross-examine as to those matters that he wishes to do so. Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. Good day to everyone, and I wish everyone a Happy Easter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Masovic.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First of all, there's something I would like to clarify for myself. I'd like to clarify something that concerns your attitude towards the Serbs and towards me personally so that I can view your testimony in that light. Do you agree that the Serbian side in Bosnia-Herzegovina was very unhappy with your attitude towards the Serbian victims?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, my answer to your question depends on what you mean when you say "the Serbian side." In the institute in which I work, there's something that could be called the Serbian side according to your logic, and all I can say is that I'm on excellent terms with my Serbian colleagues in the Institute for Missing Persons. I have in mind the board of the institute, the Serbian members, the directors' collegium, the supervisory board, and the advisory board. It is true that some members of certain non-governmental organisations for a certain period of time, for a lengthy period of time, perhaps, have been putting into dispute not only my legitimacy but also the legitimacy of Serbian members of the Institute for Missing Persons. They would point out that they are not happy with the number of individuals of Serbian nationality who have been found or identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that as far as the Serbian side is concerned, it is the families of those who were killed or went missing that are most interested in the results of the work of your institute and in your own work?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there are two different associations composed of Serbian family members of those who were killed. One of them has an HQ in Banja Luka and one of them falls in the category that you mentioned. And the second association that also assembles Serbian families who have missing family members, well, it has its HQ in Sarajevo and they fully support the work of the Institute for Missing Persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for the association with its HQ in Eastern Sarajevo, do they support your work and your attitude towards the Serbian victims in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't [Realtime transcript read in error "Kosevo Hospital"] come to the conclusion that the members of that association didn't support the work of the Institute for Missing Persons or my work. Sometimes there was some dissatisfaction that would be expressed on the whole through the media, but on the whole that association that is led by Mr. Milan Mandic supports the institute's work and the work of us who are on the board or in charge of that institute.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we see 1D5515 in the e-court system, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this criminal report submitted against you by the president of the organisation of families of the captured combatants and missing civilians? Have you ever seen this criminal report before?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: No, I haven't ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please look towards the bottom of the page on what grounds this criminal report was filed, because it says here that you had hidden ten bodies of Serb soldiers, and you covered up the whole affair as a result of which they cannot be traced. It speaks about a meeting in Doboj which was held on the 26th of May, 1997. There is mention of Sheila Barry [phoen] as an OHCR representative of Banja Luka and some other names of the people who took part in that meeting. And then in the next paragraph it is said that you had found 38 bodies and another 15 were missing, and then you managed to find them later on, but the ten bodies of the Serb soldiers had never been mentioned again nor has any information required been provided. Is this correct? Did you attend this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the parties for not having time to translate this, but I'm sure that the witness can cope excellently with the Cyrillic script.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I see in the transcript that in line 26 it says "Kosevo Hospital." I don't think that you mentioned that at all. Although I see it in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which page?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Line 21.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, this left column, what it signifies, whether it's the page number or what. So if you would go back a bit, this is completely out of the context as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, no. Not Kosevo Hospital, but it says families of those who are captured or missing or killed combatants and missing civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's just a correction that will be done to the final transcript. The word "Kosevo Hospital" should read "couldn't."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I believe that this was mentioned in the witness's answer not in my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So did this meeting take place on the 26th of May, 1997, in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot confirm the date precisely, but I do remember meeting in Doboj and I remember what was being discussed on that occasion in Doboj, and the allegations in this criminal report are absolutely baseless for a simple reason which is my colleagues from the then office for tracing missing persons unfortunately until the Institute for Missing Persons was established in 2002 had applied, I would say, a kind of inappropriate logic in that the bodies of the people who disappeared in the war should be subject of exchange. In other words, they were obliged to provide a certain number of bodies to another entity and to receive a number of bodies from that entity in return. In the then State Commission for Tracing Missing Persons we never accepted that logic. We believed that the bodies of all those who were found and had been considered missing, regardless of their status, whether they be soldiers or civilians, should be handed over to their families. This is the practice that we pursued in 1996 and that is how we do it nowadays at the Institute for Missing Persons. So if we are talking about this particular association, it is possible that this criminal report relates, although I said I'm not familiar with it, relates to a situation in which a while ago, I don't know exactly when, I gave a statement to the state agency for investigations and protection, and I suppose this is what this is all about. Although, as I said, I've never seen this document before and I clearly said what is said here, that is to say that bodies of the people who were killed cannot be subject of any calculations or arrangements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Masovic, this criminal report does not refer to exchanges of bodies but, rather, to the cover-up of the bodies of ten Serb soldiers who were allegedly hidden. This is what you were accused of, that is to say that you sabotaged the efforts of the Serbian side to locate their missing people. If we look at the bottom of the page and the next page, can you see where it says ten Serb soldiers, where it says the -- although the other side asked them -- him to do that on many occasions and the last time it was done in Banja Luka on the 18th of February in the Assembly building, and on this occasion he said, "Sue me." Did you say that? Did you say, "Sue me"?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: If we go back to the beginning of this criminal report, you will see that I was right, because it says here that there was an alleged plan to have Bosniak bodies exchanged for the alleged bodies -- ten bodies of Serb soldiers for whom the State Commission purportedly had information about their whereabouts or where they had been buried. So I ascertained that this is an attempt to carry out an exchange of dead bodies. As I said, during the war we had no other option but to act in this way, that is to say that we had to exchange bodies of both soldiers and civilians. However, after the Dayton Accords, this practice was completely discontinued on our side, and the international instruments and Dayton Accords make it incumbent on all the parties to assist the former opponent in obtaining their respective remains of soldiers and civilians. We on the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina had this attitude towards that people in 1996, and we maintain the same attitude nowadays.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you said the State Commission that purportedly had information, did you refer to the commission that you were the head of? You're not referring to the Central Commission of Republika Srpska but the State Commission of which you were the head and this commission had information about these ten people.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: No. Quite the contrary. The -- had the State Commission had any information, they would have been made available just like we did before for the colleagues from our -- from our counterparts from the office for tracing the missing persons in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But this criminal report does not speak about the exchange of 38 bodies for ten bodies but, rather, to make you afford the equal treatment for the Serb dead and that you provide them with the bodies of the ten Serb soldiers who had gone missing on the Muslim side. So this is not about the exchange but, rather, about your attitude towards the Serbs and the Serbian victims, which was extremely biased and prejudicial, and according to the allegations made by these organisations was aimed at proving that the Serbs didn't suffer as much as the other sides. What do you have to say to this?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Now, if we actually had this attitude, you would be right. It would be harmful. But I reiterate here that we never entertained this kind of attitude especially after the signing the Dayton Accords, and I agree with you that this kind of attitude would be damaging, that it would be something that would constitute discrimination against the victims and would be contrary to our laws and the international treaties signed between the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina and International Commission for Missing Persons. So this attitude was not entertained by either myself and by any of the commission ending with the federal commission and, finally, I did not do this as a member of the managing board. It was quite the contrary. Let me just give you an example that happened a couple of years ago. After the exhumation of Serbian victims in the eastern part of Herzegovina that were exhumed from a natural crevasse which was about 100 metres deep, we knew that four members of the Serbian family Vukovic were there. Members of the Special Police, they are Alpine Task Force, went down into the pit. They found the skeletal remains on a plateau down there, but then I went down into the pit and I noticed that this plateau is not actually the very bottom of the pit but that it goes even further because it was obvious that water found its way further in depth. I personally asked this Alpine group to go further down, and I also accompanied them there. We reached the depth of 100 metres, which we -- which is the place where we found the majority of bones of the Vukovic family. And I am talking about this publicly for the first time. If you read the newspapers in Bosnia-Herzegovina or if you follow electronic broadcasts, this is something that I had never said before, but I felt the need to say this today in this courtroom in order to shame the people who authored this criminal report, because contrary to their allegations, I am a person who is doing his best to participate in tracing all missing persons regardless of their ethnicity or any other affiliation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, a question was asked by Dr. Karadzic earlier on, and it could be that you missed it. Can we hear you on this: Did you, on the 18th of February, in the Assembly building, say, "Sue me"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my statement that I gave to the state agency for investigations and protection, I suppose with regard to this criminal report, I said that I did not remember that event, and I honestly cannot confirm today whether at one point in time due to the repetitive allegations that were levelled against me by the people who were politicised, if I at one point did say, "Sue me." I allow for a possibility that at one point during a meeting in Banja Luka I may have been irritated and annoyed and uttered those words, but I honestly don't remember, because this is not my nature and not the way I behave. But I allow for the possibility that those people who have written this document are telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency, for this clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, Mr. Masovic: Do we have the statement of yours given to the state agency SIP or whoever it is that you gave it to? Do we have this statement that you mentioned a minute ago?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have it, and I've never received a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We are going to ask the OTP or the agency to provide it. Thank you. Is it true, Mr. Masovic, that in your testimonies and comments and documents you used to call the Serbian side rebels?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that I used that term during the war, and in line with the Geneva Conventions and since my government believed that the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was the subject of an aggression by the Republic of Serbia and the Republic of Montenegro, so in line with the Geneva Conventions, the enemy side was called renegade or outlaw forces, and this is the term that I used throughout the war. I didn't use the term "rebels."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there a difference, legally speaking, between the warring parties and the forces that you call renegade forces? You are a trained lawyer, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're correct, I am a lawyer, an attorney by profession, but I'm not sure that I understood. If you think about -- if you're talking about members in this wartime period of renegade or outlaw forces as I referred to them, are you thinking of them? Of course there is a difference in legal status in any event, but equally as they are protected by the Geneva forces, the regular forces of the government that is in conflict, the members of the renegade or outlaw forces are protected in the same way under the Geneva Conventions. I think that's how it is if that's what you meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. But you were aware that if -- if it was the renegade forces, they are being viewed as citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina as you put it, and the very participation in combat is considered a crime and could be processed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I understand the question. People, regardless of their ethnicity, who are citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, who committed certain crimes such as illegal possession of weapons, refusal to be mobilised, assisting the enemy, killing prisoners of war, committing war crimes towards the injured, the sick, crimes to go -- towards negotiators, parliamentarians who go to negotiations was something that was prosecuted by the authorised legal institutions of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the government in Sarajevo did not distinguish here among persons of Serbian, Bosniak, or Croatian ethnicity or any other ethnicity. They were all the subject of prosecution by the authorised judicial institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My question refers to members of the Serbian armed forces, the Army of Republika Srpska. If they were captured, were they treated as prisoners of war or as criminals who would be prosecuted only because they belonged to the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the answer to that question is beyond the mandate of my expertise and my testimony. This is a question for the judicial institutions, for those who arrested, indicted, and sentenced such persons. As to the grounds of why they were arrested, prosecuted, or charged, I really don't know what the status of these persons was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, in your statement of the 30th of May, 2003, and the 2nd of June, 2003, in paragraph 22 you said that the members of the armed forces -- of enemy armed forces who were held in B and H prisons were citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina as well, and pursuant to international law, they were not treated as prisoners of war, and criminal proceedings could be initiated against them in accordance with the local laws. Is this one of the consequences of this labelling of the Serbian side as a renegade, outlaw side?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: There were two groups of people that were in prison. One group was under the category of prisoners of war. These were people who were captured in fighting, in combat, as members of the army, as member of the enemy army. As far as I know, a number of them was accused under Article 119, paragraph 1 of the Criminal Code of Bosnia and Herzegovina as members of the enemy army. I don't know if any of them were sentenced, but I know from some documents that I had the opportunity to see during the wartime period that some of them were charged under that article. The second group of people that was in prison consisted of persons de facto who were not captured during fighting but were charged with certain criminal acts that had to do with the war. These were people that I mentioned earlier. They were charged for aiding the enemy, for illegal possession of weapons and explosive devices, for espionage, not responding to mobilisation. So I'm talking about these two categories of people in the broadest possible sense. Prisoners of war or fighters who were captured at the fronts and noncombatant prisoners, people who were not in uniform, who were not captured in the front but were arrested in different places, and their arrest did have something to do with the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. So this position of yours from your statement of 2003 is something that should be changed. It should be corrected. So it is not correct that members of the enemy armed forces were in prison, that they did not have the status of prisoners of war. You said that they did not have this status and that they could be tried under the local laws.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Again, I'm saying it's my opinion, and at that moment I was not a member of the military prosecutor's office or the Military Court, and I really cannot tell you what their position was in these proceedings. But on the basis documents that I had access to, I say that some of them were charged under Article 119, which states -- or refers to participation in the enemy army. I don't know whether that means that they do have the right to the status of prisoners of war, for example, as a members of the Serbian army who happened to be in territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina would have who would undoubtedly be a prisoner of war according to Bosnian law and the Geneva Conventions or does not have the right to such a status because a person is a citizen of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is something that I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And as a lawyer, did you establish if the Geneva Conventions also applied to internal conflict?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the sense of conduct towards members of enemy formations, for members who are not foreign citizens. They enjoy equal protection that members of enemy and aggressor armies that come from a different state enjoy as well. I think that Geneva Additional Protocols grant equal or almost equal status to members of armies that take part in internal conflicts that do not spread beyond the territory of a certain state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You probably did hear about the first trial at this Tribunal, the case against Tadic. Did you notice that it was established then that the conflict does have an international character and that the Geneva Conventions Article 4 must be applied of the Geneva Conventions -- of the 3rd Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I see that Madam Sutherland is on her feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to these questions in relation to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Karadzic, this is a matter of customary international law of which the Tribunal and the Judges will take notice. The question of whether or not this particular witness did or did not understand - and it appears that he did understand - the ramifications of the law is really, certainly in my view, wasting your limited time and doesn't really assist the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. I think that it will become evident that this is relevant, that the attitude of this side towards the Serb side was different and that the Serb side was not happy with that. I don't know whether that position is the result of personal animosity or the position that Serbian members of the army are beyond the law is something that would need to be examined, but I will move to a different topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina, were they obliged to join the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how I could answer this question. I was not a member of the Ministry of Defence whose duty it was to carry out the mobilisation in wartime. So I believe that in the situation where an attack of another army of another state took place against a sovereign state, in principle then all those obliged under the law to be summoned to serve in the military should respond to that summons. I'm not speaking about Bosnia-Herzegovina now but I'm speaking generally. If one's state is attacked, all of those subject to military service duty should be summoned and they should respond to this summons because according to local laws, if they don't do that, they would be committing a crime of not responding to the call-up. This is a valid law in the former Yugoslavia, and at the moment when the war started in Bosnia and Herzegovina, this was also a valid law in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which already had its own criminal penal code and also did adapt -- adopt some provisions of the criminal law of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your statement of 2003, in paragraph 22, you also said that people were arrested because, among other things, possession of weapons not -- joining the enemy army, for armed rebellion, or refusing the call for mobilisation. Did the Muslims in Republika Srpska also have to respond to the mobilisation then? I mean, do you agree that they did not have to do this and that this was something that could be done on a purely voluntary basis?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how to answer this question. I spent the whole war in Sarajevo, and what happened outside of the territory that was under the control of the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina is something that I know about only to the extent that it applied to my activities during the war. And my activities during the war involved my duties as a member and vice-president of the State Commission for the Exchange of Captured Persons, Prisoners of War. That was my area of duty, work of that State Commission. That was the mandate of that State Commission that I belonged to during the wartime period. Whether somebody was mobilised in Republika Srpska or Srpska Republika as it was called in the early stage of the war or not, whether they were obliged to respond or not is something that I really don't know anything about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, would you agree? Did you notice that the United Nations treated us as an equal party in negotiations before the war broke out and after the war broke out as an equal party to the conflict? Did the status of the Serbian side in Bosnia and Herzegovina change as far as the United Nations was concerned in the same way that it changed as far as your side was concerned?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I never took part in these negotiations with members of the United Nations, and until the 21st of August, 1992, moreover, I was carrying on with my law practice and probably that is the period that you mean when you refer to the period before the war. As for the time during the war, I'm really not aware of how the United Nations treated, as you refer to them, the parties in the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. This will be the last question on this topic. Did the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina or you personally decide to refer to Serbs as renegades? Was this an official thing? Were you instructed by the government to call or to refer to the Serbs and to treat them as renegades or outlaws, or was this a matter of your own personal choice?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know what the government position was on the matter of how they would refer to the enemy side, but departing from the Geneva Conventions and the Additional Protocols to the Geneva Conventions, I believe that since this was not an external enemy but an enemy from Bosnia and Herzegovina that had entered into a conflict with their own government, and that was the factual state at the time when I came to the State Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners of War, that is how I did refer to members of the enemy as renegade or outlaw forces. That was my commission in the State Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners of War. Probably other members of the government or the government itself referred to members of the enemy formations differently.
