utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to look at your amalgamated statement, so I would like you to take a copy of the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps the Prosecution could provide a copy for Mr. Masovic, because now I'm going to be going through some of the paragraphs. Perhaps we can also provide the witness with a copy. We have it in Serbian. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have a look at paragraph 7, please, where reference is made to the responsibility of the State Commission and three subcommissions. Did the Serbian side have anything similar?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. I could say that they had something similar. The Serbian commission was called the Central Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners of War and I'm not sure that they had exactly the same structure. I don't know whether they had these three subcommissions, one for exchanges, for records on the killed and wounded, and then a subcommission to keep records on missing persons. So I don't know whether they had exactly the same structure, but in principle, I do know for sure that that commission did have the responsibility for getting involved in the exchange of POWs, of those who had been arrested, and of those who had been killed. As to whether they also had a mandate to make -- to keep records of those who had been killed, who had gone missing, who had been wounded, I don't know. That wasn't the subject of our discussions, the discussions that we had together in the course of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In subparagraph 8 you said that the Presidency amnestied -- granted an amnesty for certain prisoners. Do you agree that on the Serbian side there was also this attitude according to which the Presidency should grant an amnesty prior to exchange? They should grant an amnesty to those who were being prosecuted. Have you seen any documents drafted by myself that says that individuals were exchanged because I put an end to their prosecution?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, it would be correct to interpret paragraph 8 in the following way: I said for each individual case, not for each case. It's an important difference. For each individual case, if it concerned individuals who were prosecuted, who had been accused or perhaps even sentenced for certain crimes, well, in such cases it was essential to receive something from the head of state in Bosnia-Herzegovina, from the Presidency. It was necessary to receive a document stating that prosecutions would be halted -- or, rather, that amnesty would be granted to those who had been sentenced. And the Presidency did that in order to carry out exchanges of prisoners. In none of the documents that I received from my Presidency -- well, I didn't show any of these documents from the Presidency to my colleague, Dragan Bulajic, and I co-operated with him during the wartime period the most. And I also never had the occasion of seeing any of the documents that you yourself signed, not only a document on granting amnesties but any other kind of document because this quite simply wasn't an area that we were interested or involved in. For us it was important to secure certain conditions so that a given individual could be released from prison and handed over to the enemy side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you nevertheless said somewhere - I can find that - that in your opinion Karadzic sometimes took decisions. Are you aware of any decision of mine that didn't concern the granting of an amnesty in accordance with the law?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I really can't remember. In my statement I mentioned the name of someone who referred to you, who used your name and said that you were on good terms with each other. That person wasn't officially involved in the Serbian Central Commission for Exchanges, but sometimes that person did attend negotiations that were conducted in a neutral area, that were conducted at the Sarajevo airport during the war. The name of the person is Stjepan Lazarevic, and he very often said that you were on good terms, and on the basis of some Bosniaks who were released, and that was thanks to him, I gained the impression that he in fact did have a certain amount of influence within that body. And in some cases, my colleague Bulajic from the Central Commission wasn't capable of doing certain things and Mr. Lazarevic managed to do these things. How, I really don't know. But yet again let me repeat what I have said: He said that he was on good terms with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When he mentioned being on good terms with me, did that help him to be accepted as a partner? Was that in any way advantageous to him? Did it in some way demonstrate that he was reliable?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he wasn't part of the structure of the commission for exchanges, but nevertheless, he would appear together with members of the commission for exchanges and as someone from the other side involved in negotiations I took that into account. I took the fact that he was part of the team for negotiations into account because I could see that colleagues who were officially members of the Serbian Central Commission for Exchanges respected him and accepted him. There were other individuals who also attended negotiations not as frequently as Mr. Lazarevic. Sometimes they were people who were interested in their personal problems or, rather, they wanted to have personal contact with me or other members of the commission to deal with their personal problems, to establish contact with family members, or perhaps they contacted us because their family members were in prison for certain crimes, perhaps, and they were attempting to obtain their release from prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 8, you say that you were present in the Presidency when exchanges all for all were discussed, and you said that one session there was a discussion about Serb detainees in Tarcin. Does that concern the silo in Tarcin?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. One of the items of the agenda at the meeting I was present at concerned yet again an amnesty for the purpose of an exchange. It concerned an amnesty for certain individuals in prison and there was also a discussion about the status of Serbs in the prison that was popularly called the silo and this prison was located in Tarcin. So this was discussed. The status of those prisoners or captives was a matter that was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that at that session of the Presidency, President Izetbegovic said that it seemed that civilians were being kept there and that they weren't responsible for anything, they hadn't done anything? Do you remember any conclusions about that matter?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I think I'd have to have a look at the transcript at sessions of the Presidency. I was present only when there were items of the agenda that I reported on. For example, if the Presidency had ten items on their agenda and if there was an item that concerned granting amnesty and it was item 7, well, then I wasn't present when the other items were discussed. I would only arrive for the seventh item on the agenda. For example, I can't now remember which item was in fact concerned, but when my item was called out I would enter the Presidency, attend the session, and as soon as the item had been dealt with, I would leave the Presidency. So without actually seeing the transcript I can't remember whether I was present when the conclusion was adopted in relation to that item. So I can't remember what else was discussed, but I do remember that at the Presidency there was a discussion about the status of Serbians who were being kept in detention in the silo in Tarcin.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 1D5509.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when the Serbs who were being held in the silo in Tarcin were in fact released? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: They were gradually released from the prison in Tarcin, in succession, in fact. That started in 1992 and continued right up until the post-Dayton period, so to speak. In the Dayton agreement, part of the item that concerns the release of POWs and that concerns missing individuals, in that item it ordered all the sides to act within 90 days from the time of signing the agreement and by that time all POWs had to be released. If I remember this correctly, and I think I do, the last group of prisoners to be released from the prison in Tarcin was released on the 26th or 27th of January, or perhaps it was even on both those days, on the 26th and the 27th of January, 1996. So that was before this 90-day dead-line expired. And this is what had been agreed by those who had signed the Dayton peace agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. And do you know that the vast majority of prisoners in the silo spent the entire wartime period in captivity in the silo? This isn't the relevant document. This document relates to Gorazde. Are you aware of the fact that they were kept in detention in the silo throughout the war? The majority of the prisoners were kept in detention there.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean when you say "throughout the wartime period." I said that from 1992 onwards, the prisoners being held in the silo were exchanged. This was done partly through exchanges organised by the local authorities, and it was done in part through exchanges organised by the State Commission for the Exchange of POWs, but I believe that after the Dayton agreement about 100 of them were released. And if I'm not mistaken, the maximum number of detainees in the silo was over 300. So as for your question that concerns whether the majority of the prisoners were kept in the silo throughout the wartime period, well, my answer to that question would be no, if we bear these figures in mind. But, yes, some prisoners, about a hundred, I think, were still in that prison at the end of the war, rather, when the Dayton agreement was signed. Some of them remained in detention in the silo throughout that period of time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could this criminal report please be marked for identification? 1D5515 is the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I don't see any difficulty with that, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit D226 [sic]. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellencies. Could we now see 1D5506.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'd like to show two documents to you that show how the Serbian side dealt with issues of exchange -- or, rather, with granting amnesty. Do you agree that this is a decision on pardoning individuals who were sentenced? This says they're being released from the need to serve their sentence, and furthermore, it says that]they will no longer be prosecuted. It says these individuals who are of Croatian nationality will no longer be prosecuted. It says that they are being pardoned so that they can be exchanged with prisoners from the Army of Republika Srpska. So is the procedure here the same sort of procedure that the Presidency in Bosnia-Herzegovina followed?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: It's really difficult for me to draw any conclusions on the basis of this document. The only conclusion I can draw is that all the individuals who are being released here are of the same nationality. The individuals here are of Croatian nationality, and that concerns the individuals who are being released on one side and the individuals on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No. They're all from the same side, but in the case of some, one group of individuals don't -- they won't have to serve their sentence, and in the case of another group of individuals, they won't be prosecuted anymore. The first two were, in fact, sentenced. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what this document states. The individuals concerned were sentenced. They are of Croatian nationality, and it appears that they are also individuals who are being prosecuted but who have not yet been sentenced and they are individuals who are also of Croatian nationality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you have been aware of these Croats who were to be exchanged, and did you know about them? Because in May 1995, you and the HVO were not enemies. You had an established federation. Should you have been aware of this?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Up until the time when the conflict broke out between the ABiH and the HVO in October 1992, and the situation escalated in 1993, up until that time in the State Commission as a rule we were aware of these exchanges, and even if the HVO organised the exchanges, we would be aware of them. After the conflict broke out between the ABiH and the HVO, the HVO became the enemy side. And we were then no longer aware of exchanges between the HVO and the Serbian side. They would deal with those issues bilaterally, and we would be unaware of these exchanges. But as to whether I should have been familiar with -- as to whether I should have been familiar with such documents, I've already answered that. When my colleagues came to negotiate on behalf of other enemy sides, it wasn't necessary for me to provide them with documents on being granted amnesties, on being released from prison. What was important for them was that the prisoners would appear at the site of exchange and that they'd be handed over to them. They weren't interested in technical issues. They weren't interested in whether they had officially been granted amnesty or whether they had officially been pardoned, and so on and so forth. And similarly, on the other side, I wasn't interested in whether detainees who were going to be released by the enemy had been granted amnesty by the enemy. I wasn't interested in whether they had been prosecuted. This wasn't a matter of interest for us. Our task in the State Commission after we had taken charge of former prisoners or detainees at a confrontation line or in some neutral area, we wanted to have a brief statement from them about the conditions in the prison that they had been held in. We were interested in obtaining certain details from them that concerned the number of detainees remaining in the prison or the camp. We wanted to know whether these prisoners or detainees were being maltreated. We wanted to know what they thought about their status. We wanted to know who they thought should be exchanged immediately when another exchange was organised. They would then go to the police force and provide detailed statements about everything that they were familiar with in the territory that they had come from, in areas that they inhabited, about the conditions in prison or camp. They would provide information on whether they had witnessed cases of violations of international law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have to be a little more expeditious. I didn't ask you whether you were familiar with the document but whether you were familiar with the fact that these people had been exchanged.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 1D5507 and then I will tender both of these documents. 1D5507. And I believe that the next document will -- we'll see is one that you are probably familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, I'm not asking you about the document. I'm asking you if you knew that they were exchanged. Can we agree that we have people here who were serving a sentence but for the purpose of exchange were subject to amnesty, and all of these Muslims, as you probably have noticed, were exchanged; is that correct.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I recognise their names, and I know that this is a group of civilians from Banja Luka who worked for a Muslim humanitarian organisation and who had been providing food and other necessities for Bosniaks in Banja Luka, and that was the reason why they were arrested. I'm talking about this on the basis of the direct knowledge, because I talked to some of them. For example, I talked to Mrs. Suhreta Djuzel. That's the last name on the list. And she confirmed all I'm telling you now. Although I see this document for the first time, I can say that it shows that they had been convicted and sentenced. And it is said in this document signed by you that they would be exchanged for combatants of the Army of Republika Srpska, but, as I said, this is a group of civilians working for a humanitarian organisation in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know what this humanitarian organisation was actually doing, and do you know that a court passed a judgement about that?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I told you what I heard from Mrs. Suhreta Djuzel. Mr. Gojacic. I think I also talked to Mr. Smail. I recognise another name, that of Zijahudin Smajlovic. I think he's the man who managed to receive compensation for the entire period that he spent in your prison, and this compensation was awarded to him through a court judgement. I don't think that I talked to him, but I think that Zijahudin Smajlovic was someone who managed to get damages due to wrongful arrest, because after the war, he filed a suit for pecuniary and other damages on the basis of wrongful detention. I have some reservations about this, because this is what I learned from the media, and I didn't talk to him personally, but this name rings a bell and I think that I read about this suit in the papers. I said that I spoke with Mr. Gojacic, number 4 on the list, and Mrs. Suhreta Djuzel, number 6, also Smail Djuzel, and I think that Suhreta and Smail are actually spouses. And I talked to them after their release. And of course, I talked to them on several occasions after the end of the war. Mr. Gojacic was for a period of time the leader of the association of detention prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: After the break we are going to show you documents relating to the aforementioned humanitarian organisation. Now, I would like to draw your attention to paragraph 10 and let me ask you this: Were there those so-called private exchanges that were conducted below the radar that you didn't know anything about? And I kindly ask you to give me as brief an answer as possible, because I am pressed for time.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you can see that as far as the situations that were within my scope of responsibility, I know a lot. However, private exchanging were beyond the scope of my responsibility. I have to say that occasionally I received information that some individuals organised exchanges, this sort of private exchanges either for money or for other gain. However, they did not involve large numbers of people. It was never ten people who were exchanged but, rather, two or three relatives of somebody who managed through private channels to establish contact with the other side or one-for-one exchanges, et cetera. And I dare say that this number is insignificant in comparison to a total number of those exchanged during the war. Therefore, I cannot give you a precise answer because sometimes these private exchanges did not involve prisoners at all, because private individuals did not have access to detainees in prisons. This would usually involve people who were actually not arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, if we look at paragraph 11, I wonder if everything that you are telling me --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But before that, I'm sorry, Your Excellency, could these two documents be admitted into evidence, the ones that speak about the amnesty?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, the problem arises again of untranslated documents. Time and time again you've been warned that there will come a stage when untranslated documents are simply not going to be acceptable, and for the moment these will be admitted subject to anything the Prosecution has to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, in relation to the first document, the witness -- the only thing the witness said was he could only draw a conclusion that they were all of the same nationality from just reading the names on the document and the fact that they were released, and that was also just reading what was contained on the document. He didn't actually speak to anything other than that. And the Prosecution would like to know the provenance of these two documents, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Dr. Karadzic, you must provide suitable provenance. Very limited basis upon which they can be admitted as Ms. Sutherland points out. On the first document it's -- it's purely to the answer that the witness gave for no other purpose. Indeed, with an untranslated document it's only the answers to specific questions that are going to be taken into account by the Tribunal even when the document is translated. The whole of the document isn't going to fall into evidence. But for the present these documents can be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 1D5506 is Exhibit D2227, marked for identification; and 65 ter number 1D5507 is Exhibit P -- sorry, D2228, marked for identification. And just to correct the transcript, page 56, line 1, should read D2226. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just briefly, Your Excellencies. These are authentic documents that I signed. They have a register number and the seal of the president, and my friends who managed to get hold of the copies of these documents are currently correcting [as interpreted] them because the original archive has gone missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you this, Mr. Masovic: When you say the Serbs often killed captured military prisoners --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, one moment. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic mentioned a moment ago that he has friends who managed to get hold of the copies of these documents and they're currently correcting them because the original archive has gone missing. We have some problems with that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The interpreters said "collecting them."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Collected. I suppose -- it was collected, not corrected.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the second point is: Mr. Karadzic, would he like to share with the Court who his friends are who managed to get hold of the copies of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, that's going to be all part of the provenance that's going to be required in exactly the same way that the Prosecution would be required to show a source.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, I would like to know how did you arrive at the conclusion that Serbs often killed captured military prisoners? And I'm quoting from paragraph 11. And that concerns me a little. You told us a minute ago that you can testify about certain things, but it seems that you're capable of testifying about other things as well. This is a very broad statement and the Defence is challenging it. Can you tell me how did you establish this?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: This paragraph speaks about the reasons why the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina or Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina had to set up special departments for prisoners of war. They did this because they were satisfied with the fact that the vast majority of exchanged Bosniaks and earlier Croats were not members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina but civilians. The BH Army thought that members of the military should be involved in exchanges in as large numbers as possible, and for that purpose each corps of the BH Army established their own departments for that, and you can see here that on several occasions, especially in the earlier stages, they organised exchanges without the participation of the commission that I was a member of. Now, how I arrived at the conclusion that there were only a few members of the military, the reason is very simple. For example, a number of members of the BH Army spoke about how their fellow combatants were captured in combat at Treskavica and other places, and later on we received their dead bodies in exchange. We didn't get them alive. And there are other similar people -- examples, but I cannot remember right now. However, it will be easy to find specific examples which testify that members of the BH Army were very seldom subject of exchange of living persons but very often the exchange of dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does your amalgamated statement deal with this or did you just insert this statement offhand?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I gave you an answer to that. I just answered your question. On the basis of the fact that the majority of bodies exchanged during the war were actually members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that the number of living exchange -- exchange of living members of BH Army is insignificant as compared to that of dead bodies led me to conclude that the majority of members of the BH Army did not live to see the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Chamber now according to what you know, how many members of the BH Army did the Serbs hold in 1992? Just recall the prisons of Manjaca, Batkovici, and tell me how many combatants were captured by the Serbian Army, combatants from the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: According to what was testified by exchanged detainees, it turns out the majority of the captives were civilians, that only a very, very limited number of members of the BH Army or TO were among them. And they were captured during combat operation. The vast majority in the camps and prisons, particularly in 1992, were Bosniak and Croat and Roma civilians and civilians from other ethnic communities, including the Serbs who did not display loyalty towards the Serbian Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But how do you know that, Mr. Masovic? Based only on what you heard from other people?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Based on what was reported by members of their families when they reported missing persons, and based on what those who survived told us after they had left camps and prisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we agree --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, we'll take a break there and resume again at 1.30.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, if I may say, this witness is much too important, and I have given -- I've been given a little time. I'm hopeful that I'm going to get at least one more session tomorrow after the videolink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, we'll consider that proposition depending on how concise and relevant the cross-examination is from now on. 1.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, reviewing the witness schedule for this week, it's going to actually be extremely difficult to extend this witness's evidence beyond today except for a very small amount of time which we will try and add to today's hearing if -- with the indulgence of all the staff. So I would really endorse you to be as concise as you can be.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, may we go briefly into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm going to do my best to such my questions in such a way that you are able to answer with a yes or a no, and of course you are free to add whatever you feel is necessary. Do you agree that Mr. Izetbegovic was undoubtedly the leader of the Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina, to say the least?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Izetbegovic was the member of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and later the -- a member of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question, let me be open, was more directed in the sense of this: Do you believe that in a -- that the military conscripts did not respond to several call-ups?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to your question. And I repeat, up until the 21st of August, 1992, I was still working in my legal practice. I don't know anything about what was going on with the government when the call-ups were issued or how many people responded to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know that at least in the first year as many as 85 per cent of Muslim fighters were participating in the war in civilian clothing and that this is information that was issued by the command of that army?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no, I really don't know anything about that. That was not something that I was interested in. It was not a subject that I was following.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that the HVO let you know that all able-bodied Muslims in -- it considered all able-bodied Muslims as military conscripts during times of mobilisation, and that is how the Croatian Army or the HVO behaved during that time?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't have any contacts with the HVO, and if I did, they were very, very brief. In contacts with the service for exchange of the HVO which I was in contact with during the wartime period, I do not recall anybody telling me that in any way. It is true, though, that Mr. Pusic, who is here, Berislav Pusic, once or twice told me verbally that he personally considered all Bosniaks, or as he put it, all Muslims of the age of 16 up until the age of 70 as soldiers of the enemy army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And he personally had that position as the president of the HVO exchange commission; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if he said that in that capacity or whether that is his own personal position. It's something that I -- I don't know, but he probably wanted in that way to justify the fact that HVO camps had a large number of civilians who had nothing to do with combat. I assume that in that way he wished to justify the fact that civilian persons were being held in captivity, civilians who did not participate in combat actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you testified about this in the Prlic et al. case, and you confirmed it also in your statement of 2004, saying that the HVO, the HVO commission, stated its terms for one-on-one exchange, and for the government in Sarajevo this was always a problem, because the Bosnian Serbs and Bosnian Croats in the -- in their camps had civilians. How many Muslims lived in Kljuc, for example, according to your information? Or let me help you so that we can have yes or no answers. Do you agree that there were a bit more than 18.000 Muslims living in the Kljuc municipality?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know how many Bosniaks were there, or, as you call them, Muslims there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you agree that about 1.000 Muslims from Kljuc were captured and taken to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have that information. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if in your statements you say that Serbs were holding Muslims captive, did you work out why it wasn't the entire 18.000 of them? Why was it only a thousand? If civilians were being held in captivity, why was it only 1.000 civilians and not all of them? What was the reason why such and such a number out of a total number of Muslims in Kljuc were captured?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is something that you said. I didn't confirm what you say, so I cannot really comment on your questions. You said that 18.000 Muslim lived in Kljuc and that 1.000 of them were taken to Manjaca. This is something that I really don't know and I don't dare comment on something that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As of August on, were you dealing with the number of captured, detained Muslims?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I was working with the first and last names of the people who were in enemy camps and prisons. My goal was to release as many people as possible from those prisons and camps. It didn't matter whether they were soldiers, civilians, a man, a woman, a child. The fact is that most of them were Bosniaks in the Serbian camps and that is why the Bosniaks were the most numerous subjects of exchange. But it's also a fact that I was also dealing with Mr. Vladimir Srebrov during the war who is not a Bosniak, who is a Serb or a Montenegrin. I'm not sure how he declared himself. He was in the Kula prison and who was also a topic of my interest in the process of exchange, and finally we did manage to exchange him after a long, long period of captivity, it's true, that he spent in the Kula prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that in your statement, and you said that he was arrested because he was asking for me to be able to negotiate on a cease-fire. If I were to tell you that he was arrested because he had come to the front line to persuade the Serbs at the front line in Ilidza to leave before they were attacked, is that something different from the information that you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Srebrov was my neighbour in Sarajevo. I did mention that in my statement, and what I was saying about him going to talk to you is information that dates from that time from what he stated to the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know that Mr. Srebrov was the only member of the SDS that we ejected? We threw him out, and we did that because he was threatening that the Mlada Bosna which he was leading would become the iron fist? And then he stayed to live with you and then he began to serve in the cause?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know any of that information. I don't even know that he was a member of the SDS as you say. I don't know any of the other things you mentioned either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you are talking quite generally about how the Serbs were killing prisoners of war -- or, rather, prisoners in prisons and among other places you mention Manjaca. According to what you know, how many prisoners were killed in Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have the exact information. Prisoners in Manjaca were killed. A number of them were killed in the camp. This is testimony of those who managed to leave the camp. A number of them were taken out of the camp and at different locations at various distances from Manjaca they were killed. There are testimonies about this, and this was also established in some trials also, but I am unable to give you the precise numbers of people who were killed in the camp or outside of the camp or on their way to the camp or on their way out of the Manjaca camp to other destinations. I don't have that information. A significant number of them, I cannot give you a precise number, I'm not prepared for that, but a large number of them are still considered to be missing, people who according to the statements of their families or other inmates were last seen in the Manjaca camp and 20 years today after they were in the camps their fate is still not known. They're probably dead, because if they were alive, they would have returned to their families. They're probably dead, but their remains have still not been found.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, are you aware of the fact that throughout that period of time Manjaca was under the control of the International Red Cross? They would visit the camp at least once a week and sometimes twice, and they were all released and allowed to go to foreign countries on the 8th of December, 1992. Were you aware of that? And this is the reason for which you do not have the bodies of any of these people.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid that your statement doesn't correspond to the facts. I know for a fact that according to information provided by the ICRC, information that you are referring to, about 500 camp inmates were transferred to the Batkovici camp when Manjaca was closed down or allegedly closed down. I personally participated in negotiations that concerned the release -- or, rather, liberation of those 500 prisoners. They were mainly Bosniaks, Croats, and there was a smaller number of members of the Roma community, and they were between 18 and 65 years of age. Among them there was also a group of about 100 inmates from a place called Grapska in the vicinity of Doboj, and they passed through the Doboj prison and then they went to Manjaca, then Batkovic, Kula, Sarajevo, the Rudo prison, and they were in the Kula in Sarajevo again, and finally they were exchanged, if I'm not mistaken, in 1994. And I know that at least 11 of them were killed during their detention in Kula.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you provide the Chamber or the Prosecution, if you're not willing to do so for the Defence, could you provide them with a list of the individuals you are searching for, a list of the individuals who were in Manjaca and whom you are searching for.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's quite possible, but there is one restriction I mentioned at the beginning of my testimony when answering a question put to me by the Prosecution. This information as to where and when someone was present is usually information that is obtained from their family members. So if that information -- if such data is reliable, well, you can have such information. In the majority of cases it is the families that determine the date on which someone went missing, whether that date is correct or not. But in the records that we keep, the place where someone went missing or the place where someone used to be present is referred to as the Manjaca camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll now present you with my claim. First of all, there were 4.004 prisoners in Manjaca, five -- there were five who died, three of natural causes and two were killed as a result of being beaten up. We don't know whether this was a real intention, but people were sentenced. So there were two deaths, two individuals who were killed. Manjaca was under the constant supervision of the ICRC, as well as Batkovici. Those who had to be prosecuted were taken to Manjaca. Everyone else was taken to other countries. Do you have such information, and do you know who the individuals who went to other countries are, in fact? For the benefit of the other participants, KDZ163 is the number of a witness who testified here about the five deaths that occurred there, and this Prosecution witness was in a position to have such information.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: During the war, the State Commission for Exchanges was interested in those who were in Manjaca, not those who were released and went to other countries. No records were kept for these individuals because they weren't involved in exchanges through the State Commission. In the post-war period, we investigated cases of individuals from Manjaca who didn't survive the war or their detention in the camp, who are still listed as missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you bringing into question my claim, my claim that I unilaterally released about 4.000 individuals from Manjaca so that they could be taken to other countries?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what the answer to your question would be in a certain sense. I'm surprised by a certain fact which I wasn't aware of during the war. I'm surprised by the fact that there were as many as 4.000 people in the camp of Manjaca at one point in time. I never had such information according to which there were even 4.000 inmates in the Manjaca camp at one point in time, and that is what you are claiming. So I know nothing about your allegations according to which these people were released.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, perhaps I wasn't precise. It wasn't at one point in time but during a four-month period 4.000 individuals passed through the camp. Five individuals died, three of natural causes and two died as a result of beatings. We don't know whether this was intentional or not. But you know -- or you do know that I released everyone in Manjaca at the beginning of December and the Red Cross took them to other countries. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at that time, I was concerned with those who had not left Manjaca. The State Commission was interested in prisoners, not in those who were released. I was interested in the fate of the 500 people from Manjaca. The International Committee of the Red Cross told us that these people had not been released but that they had been transferred to the Batkovic camp. And I believe that the International Committee of the Red Cross even lodged a protest with the Serbian authorities. If I can remember this correctly, this was a long time ago, they lodged some kind of protest because of the fact that these 500 inmates had been transferred from one camp to another camp, to the camp in Batkovici. I'm not denying this fact. I'm really not aware of whether you took such a decision or not of whether these people were released or not. There's nothing I can comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, it's not 500 but significantly less, and the lists of individuals were handed over to the Red Cross, and they were registered. They arrived in Batkovici. Are you aware of the fact that they were permanently referred to on the Red Cross list or included in the Red Cross's list?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Let me repeat what I have said. I knew that they were transferred to Manjaca for the simple reason that I subsequently personally participated in the negotiations that were conducted with the Serbian commission, negotiations that concerned the release of those 500 people. The largest group was from Doboj, if I remember this correctly. There were about a hundred of them. There were also people from Jajce and from some other towns in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I personally participated in the negotiations. I participated in the procedure for their release. Some of them were released in Sarajevo, because in the end, after Batkovici, they ended up in prison in the correctional facility Kula. I cannot really say whether they were included on the list, whether records were kept about them or on the Red Cross's lists because this is confidential information and the ICRC doesn't share such information with third parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you were involved in investigations into the missing after the war, do you know anything about who is in -- is now present in third countries? I'm referring to citizens from Bosnia and Herzegovina, or at least to the Muslims? Did you in fact find out that some of those who were on your list were, in fact, now living in third countries?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know who is now living abroad, which citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina regardless of the nationality are now living abroad, but we do have contact with the families of those who have gone missing. We have contact with the International Committee of the Red Cross. We also have contact with the International Commission for Missing Persons, and we have contact with the local branch of the Red Cross in Bosnia and Herzegovina. They have their own records on those who have gone missing. We've included these lists in our commission, and on that basis - and you can see that in my report - we compiled a single database on those who who are missing in Bosnia-Herzegovina. What I could additionally say in response to your question is this: Since you say that there are people who are still alive and who are on the lists, yes, I can confirm those allegations. To date about 236 such individuals of all nationalities have been found, and at one point in time, usually in the early summer or autumn of 1992, their families reported them as missing and although they returned to their families or moved out of the country, this was never reported. So they were still included on the list of those missing because their families didn't report the fact that they weren't, in fact, missing anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you draw the conclusion that there were no more survivors but that they were on your list?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I can't say that we might have certain people recorded as missing on our list, but they are in fact living somewhere else in the world. Recently we discovered that there was a girl, a young girl who had been transferred from the northern part of Bosnia-Herzegovina to Serbia. She was two years old at the time and she was adopted by a family there. That child wasn't aware of its origins, of who its parents were. It recently came of age, and it -- the child has discovered its identity and about two years ago she returned to Bosnia and Herzegovina having discovered what her real identity was. Her name is Senada Becirevic. In Serbia her name was Mila Becirevic. That was in fact the surname of the parents who adopted her. So I can't say that tomorrow or in one year's time there won't be a similar case. I can't claim that someone might be found who is, in fact, alive but is nevertheless still included on the list of those who are missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that there were all these adults who lived in Novi Sad throughout the war and then they returned, and when they returned, they found that their names were inscribed on tombstones? Or there was the third son of a man from Bratunac, and according to the records, this son was missing, but he had in fact returned. Were you aware of these cases? There are at least two such cases that concern adults. They were both in Serbia. They lived their lives there, got married, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: If you go back to my statement, I said that I was aware of three attempts to falsely report certain individuals as missing. One of the cases is in fact the case that you are mentioning. It concerns a man who spent the war in Novi Sad or in the vicinity of Novi Sad. He was married to a Serbian woman, and his father reported him as missing as well as two other sons who really went missing, but this individual was never missing, and we believe that his father was also aware of his fate, that is to say, he was aware of the fact that he was alive and living in Serbia or, rather, in Vojvodina, but probably for certain pragmatic reasons of his own he also reported that as son as missing. So that is one of the three attempts to make a false report about someone who went missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In what way could he have benefitted from that?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, prior to 2004, he couldn't have gained any advantage from the fact, because in 2004, a Law on Missing Persons in Bosnia-Herzegovina was adopted, a law which granted the families of such missing people certain rights. For example, free education for their children, free social security, the right to learn about the fate of their family members who went missing. And Bosnia-Herzegovina established, in fact, a commission for missing persons. According to the law, there's also some sort of remuneration for the families of those who were missing, and the fund for missing persons is supposed to pay such benefits. Unfortunately, my state has been criticised for many years now, by the United Nations and other groups, because that law on financial compensation for families of missing persons was never implemented. None of the families of those missing in Bosnia-Herzegovina, regardless of their nationality, managed to receive a single euro from the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, although according to the Law on Missing Persons, the families of missing persons do have such a right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does Bosnia and Herzegovina have any lists on people who are refugees in other countries, and have you compared these lists to see whether these individuals are, in fact, alive?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether the state has any such lists. I don't believe that's the case. The Institute for Missing Persons, in any event, doesn't have such lists. They are of no importance for us, because the contact we have is contact with family members who are searching for other missing family members. So above all, we have contact with such people and there are over 9.000 such people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. They provided a drop of blood so that a DNA analysis could be used to see whether any of the victims in mass graves, in individual graves, are in fact family members of theirs. We have information from the ICRC on over 22.000 citizens from Bosnia-Herzegovina whose families are in Bosnia-Herzegovina and throughout the world. Wherever the ICRC is present, and the ICRC is mostly present in all the countries throughout the world through local Red Cross branches, we in fact submitted requests to these ICRC branches to locate these individuals. We are also in direct contact with families who are looking for their relatives who have gone missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It seems that I am putting rather extensive questions to you. Now I'm going to try and put short questions to you and elicit a yes or no answer from you if possible. So you confirmed that a large number of people changed the status of their family members in their various statements, sometimes claiming that they were dead and sometimes claiming the contrary, but it seems that according to what you think about this matter, the number of the civilians who got killed is exaggerated. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, the people who reported people missing didn't change their statement. When they originally filed reports about missing persons, they defined them as either being a soldier or a civilian. We as an institution consider this to be completely irrelevant. We don't care whether those people were civilians or soldiers. That was absolutely beyond the scope of our interest. We see them solely as missing persons, as missing citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and our mandate is to identify them and to hand over them to their families. Now, whether some of the families, but I don't know how many of them because we don't have a database specifying who was a soldier and who wasn't, and I said that was totally irrelevant, that was not our remit, we didn't care whether anyone went missing during combat operations or as a civilian. Our objective was to locate those persons and hand them over to their families. And, yes, you are right when you say that there are such reports that you have mentioned, but I cannot tell you at the moment how many of those people changed the status of the missing persons. I know that when I communicated with people during the war, I know that people reported their missing soldiers specifically to the ICRC as civilians, because they believed that would be an easier way to release them from captivity, but I'm sure that many more people actually reported their family members as soldiers but that they were actually civilians, but I cannot give you any figure, whether there were hundreds of them or many more than that, because that was not the subject of our interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, that would help me to abandon finally this line of questioning, because there's a lot being said in your statements about civilians. So can I then conclude that your statements did not focus on the fact whether someone was a civilian or a soldier, and can we then, in view of that, move to the number of those who were exhumed.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: All I can do is to repeat what I said. We who are tracing and trying to track what happened with someone is completely irrelevant whether that person was a soldier or a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me this: The authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina, including the State Commission, when did they receive initial accurate information about the people who perished in Srebrenica in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I think that about two weeks after July 1995 -- actually, that was the time when women and children left Srebrenica and arrived in Tuzla, and that is the time when they started reporting male members of their family who remained in Srebrenica. Therefore, the number of the people who went missing in July 1995 coincide actually with the arrival dates of the people who were expelled from Srebrenica. They were the first ones who provided information about their fathers, their brothers, and other male members of their families failed to cross over to the free territory, and that initiated an investigation about their fate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us very briefly: In your opinion, how many people died in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I will give you a few pieces of information. On the memorial plaque in Potocari, there are 8.372 names of the people whose death is connected with the events in Srebrenica and later with the events in Zepa. Of course, those who perished in Zepa is significantly lower. So the total number is 8.372. In the Institute for Missing Persons, we have information about 8.262 individuals whose fate and whose death is connected with Srebrenica in 1995. The International Commission for Missing Persons who is in charge pursuant to an international agreement that it signed with the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina of identifying all the exhumed victims, their estimate is that the number of the missing or those killed was 1 -- 8.100, and they reached this figure on the basis of blood samples that they had received from families. I don't know if anyone produced this figure before. I did because I'm aware of that information, being a member of the managing board. The ICRC collected mother than 22.000 blood samples from family members of the people from Srebrenica. These 22.000 blood samples relate to a total of 7.800 people who went missing in Srebrenica, and I think that the exact number is 7.787. However, nowadays in the ICP, there's more than 160 DNA reports that do not match with a single blood sample out of the 22.000. What does that mean? That means that there are families in Srebrenica who either didn't provide blood samples, or that there is not a single survivor from this family who could provide a blood sample, which means that either all of them were killed during the events in Srebrenica or that quite simply this family has no survivors left. If you take the figure of 7.787 and if you add, I think, 166 of those who were exhumed from mass graves where the Srebrenica victims were found but for whom no matches were found, a total number is about 8.000. And as I said, the estimate of ICP is that 8.100 people disappeared during the events in Srebrenica in 1995. And in my view, I think that this estimate is the closest to figure of 8.262 which is the number that our institute operates with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: According to what you know, how many inhabitants were there in Srebrenica in July 1995 before these events took place?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please repeat the answer. The mike didn't switch on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. Can you repeat that, please. There's no interpretation because the microphone was not on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, and I don't think if it is appropriate for me to speak about this as a witness, but I know that there were figures mentioned in the media of 30.000 to 40.000 people living in Srebrenica. Whether they were the natives of Srebrenica, whether they were the people who in 1992 came to Srebrenica from other municipalities such as Bratunac, Zvornik, Rogatica, Vlasenica, and other municipalities, that in 1992 the Bosniaks were either persecuted or killed or et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please let's stick to the briefest possible answers. Shall I infer from your previous answer that the ICRC has matches for 7.800 people according to the samples?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: No. The ICMP has somewhat more than 6.600 matches, plus the 166 in which they obtained DNA profiles but did not find any matches. So we can say that these 166 individuals have no names because their unique DNA profiles are different from everybody else. And I said that on the basis of the blood sample provided by the family.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. This is interesting but we don't have time for that. Is it correct that you established that at least 500 people were buried in Potocari and that they are unrelated to the events in Srebrenica in 1995? I said 500, yes? 500, that's right.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: No, that is not correct, and nobody credible or relevant stated that 500 people were buried in Potocari and that they had nothing to do with what happened in Srebrenica in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that either you or someone from your profession stated that there were several hundred people who were alive but that their severed limbs were identified based on the DNA? This is something that somebody said about a month ago?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I said, but it doesn't relate to Srebrenica. It pertains to a cemetery in Sarajevo. My colleagues from the Banja Luka office wanted an examination of severed limbs and stillborn babies to be conducted that were buried there. I'm sure that they exhumed severed parts of the bodies and stillborn people by mistake, not intentionally. Those were the amputated limbs and stillborn children had been brought from a hospital, and unfortunately they have been kept in a morgue in Sarajevo for years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Please give me short answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have now 1D5516, and we don't have much time. I apologise. It hasn't been translated because I didn't expect this witness to confirm this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please look these red boxes. It says: "Amor Masovic, the director of the Institute for Missing Persons, also confirmed that at the memorial centre there are victims who are next of kin of those already buried and identified as the victims of the Srebrenica crime. We fulfil the requests of the families and the mothers who for sentimental and emotional reasons asked for permission to have their sons who was killed in 1993 be buried next to the son who was killed in the genocide in Srebrenica. He said that because of that practice, they soon faced the possibility that there wouldn't be enough space for the burials of the Srebrenica victims." Did you state this?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is true that in the memorial complex in Potocari, in addition to the victims from Srebrenica July 1995, a number of their next of kin such as brothers and fathers are also buried there, and they were buried there on the basis of being related to the victims of Srebrenica, and thanks to the efforts of the foundation and the Council of Ministers of Bosnia-Herzegovina, permission was granted for two brothers, one of whom died in 1992, the other one who died in 1995, that they both could be buried in the same memorial complex. What is important is to say that those killed in 1992 are not reckoned as the victims who died in 1995. They don't belong to the same group. When I mentioned the figures 8.362 and 8.372, I was speaking only about those who were victims from July 1995. I'm not talking about these people who died in 1992 or 1993. Now, the foundation of the memorial complex is facing a possibility that based on the kinship, hundreds of thousands of those who were killed in 1995 cannot be buried there any longer because there is not enough space for that. And they said that those 70 that had been buried here will remain there, but in future no such burials will be allowed irrespective of the fact that are brothers and sons, grandfathers and fathers, et cetera. So what I said here is completely accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D5024, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting, Mr. Masovic, do you know how many people were killed in that area from 1992 until 1995?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: People who were killed in that area, I assume you mean Srebrenica, the Srebrenica enclave, were most probably buried by their families, and they were never the topic of interest of the previous State Commission, nor are they now subject of interest of the institute, because they do not have the status of a missing person. So I don't know how many people were killed in and around Srebrenica or in any other municipality in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is not part of our mandate. These are not missing persons so that I would be interested in finding out their fate or their number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And are you saying that when a Serb is killed in Muslim territory or a Muslim in Serb territory that they would be handed over to their family for burial, or would they be buried by the opposing side while they would be recorded in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina records or in the records of the Army of Republika Srpska even though they were buried by someone else, by the other side?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how you mean buried by the other side. If they were killed, conditionally speaking, in their own territory, then they would be buried by their family, and they would not be reported as a missing person. If they were killed in enemy, conditionally speaking, territory, then the family would report that person as a missing person, because they don't know what their fate was. They don't know if he's dead, alive, in captivity. Then they would report that person as a missing person. That's the principle. Perhaps some families found out about the fact of death occurring in enemy territory so they did not report the person as missing, because through certain contacts with people from the other side they learned that their relative, family member was killed, died, is buried in such and such a place, and therefore there was no need for them to report that person as a missing person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that after the liberation or the capture, however you want to put it, of Podrinje, they found in 1993 about 50 mass graves numbering from 50 -- from 5 to 50 bodies. This was found by the Serbs, which was actually in the territory which was controlled by the Muslims before? Do you know or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm just waiting for the transcript. Actually, I don't know. This is the first time that I'm hearing about this, from you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting but there's a document on the screen and I don't know if it's 1D5024, but if it is, it wasn't on the list of documents for cross-examination and I don't know whether there's a translation that's available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Can you assist, Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was expect Mr. Masovic to confirm the numbers, so I was not planning to tender it, but now I am forced to show it. Can we look at page 6, please, in that case, and I kindly ask for the understanding of the other side in the same way that I show understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, it doesn't actually answer Ms. Sutherland's query.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I wasn't intending to put it on the list, Your Excellency, because I believed that the witness would confirm the numbers. That's why I did not announce this document. So I wasn't planning to show the list if the witness confirmed the numbers. I would now kindly like to ask the witness if -- can we scroll up a little bit please. Whether it's correct that President Izetbegovic was confirming that there were 4.500 people there, soldiers there without the Zepa Brigade. There was a review of the 28th Division, and 3.500 people gathered in Tuzla. However, a little bit lower down, Silajdzic says, well, here this is what it's about. First in Srebrenica they were giving another number for UNPROFOR and we knew a different one, and the president says 42.000 for UNPROFOR and 35.000 realistically. So there were 35.000 people in Srebrenica realistically speaking. Can we look at the next page. This is on the 11th of August, a month after the fall of Srebrenica. And can you look to see how many people went to Tuzla? Thirty-one thousand, 31.000, while 1.000 -- it says 600 to 650, well, we know that 1.000 went to Serbia via Zepa, meaning that 32.000 people are in question, and 3 to 4 people are missing. And look at what the president says at the bottom: The figure of those killed is probably around 3.000 people. This is the number that has been referred to from the very first days there, namely, we intercepted a very clear Chetnik telephone conversation where you can see that it's authentic, and it says: There was a massacre here yesterday. It was a real slaughterhouse. Hey, how many, 300? No. Add one more 0, and so on and so forth. And can we look at the next page -- I'm sorry. Pardon me. Just a moment. I'm talking about the total number. Silajdzic says, I'm talking about total number. I'm afraid that this number of 5.000, the fact is that when we were in Kalesija I heard that there was a massacre. There's no doubt about that. You probably know that mass graves can be discovered by satellite and so on and so forth. And then he says something about Karadzic, and he says, If we quarrel with them, we will have no chance, so we're playing a little game here. So according to these estimates, it would be 5.000 whose fate is uncertain, out of them 2.000 casualties. For 3.000 there's still probably some hope that some of them are in camps, that some are still trying to break through. Some of them went towards Zepa. Probably the number of casualties is around 3.000, and this is according to a Chetnik report which in this case could be the most authoritative one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Therefore, Mr. Masovic, the country's Presidency one month after the fall of Srebrenica knows that 3 -- 31.000 people reached Tuzla, that 670 went via Zepa, and that 2.000 more were still wandering around in the woods, and we do have evidence about that, that groups remained there for a long time. How can you then talk about 7- to 8.000 casualties in July?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: What you are saying that the Presidency knows is something that I don't know. I know something else. So far in more than 450 locations connected to July 1995, at least 6.800 complete or incomplete skeletal remains of victims of Srebrenica were found. These were people reported as missing by their families. So far 8.262 people were reported missing by their families. These are Srebrenica victims. I know this today, 15 or 16 years after July 1995, because this is exact data and it's derived directly from mass graves. Unfortunately, at least a half of those graves are secondary graves. And I have to say an astonishing fact as well, a man from Srebrenica or remains of him were found in four different mass graves. His head and his arms were found in the Zeleni Jadar 4 grave. His right leg or thigh were found in Glogova 01 grave, the right tibia belonging to this man was found in the Bljeceva 03 grave, and his left complete leg, the femur, the tibia and the fibula were found in Budak 02 grave. These four graves are in the territory of two different municipalities, in the Srebrenica municipality, and the Bratunac municipality area, and what is the worst, the body of that victim is still not complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Can you please answer with a yes or no. Now, do you know that before July 1995 the 28th Division had more than 2.000 casualties, dead, about 2.000 dead? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: No. That is not the subject of my interest. It wasn't something that I was looking at then or something that I'm looking at now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to tell you that the vast majority, up to 90 per cent, of Muslims were fighters, were killed in Serbian territory and buried in Serbian territory, would this be something that would be understandable in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you consider Serbian territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Under Serbian control.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, that's a little different. So they were killed in the towns and villages where they lived, I assume. Unfortunately, they were buried in places other than their places of residency in primary graves, then they were relocated to secondary and tertiary graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm talking about the 28th Division which was going out to Serbian areas, out of the protected area, out of the safe area, and it lost over 2.000 people. None of those people was killed in the territory under the control of the Muslims but in territory under the control of the Serbs. Do you know where these soldiers, these people, were buried?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Which time period are you thinking of in your question throughout the whole war?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, throughout the whole war, especially from 1993 when the safe area was declared. These people were killed outside of the enclave, not within the enclave. Where were they buried?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: But this simply cannot be true. This means that their families did not want to report that they were missing to the then State Commission. None of those 2.000 -- well, I'm not going to say none, but you're talking about a thousand -- thousands of people. I'm saying that people who were either civilians or soldiers who were killed in the territory under the control of the Serbs were not reported as missing, and that's not plausible. If they were killed in areas under the control of the Serbian people, it would be logical for their command if not their families to report them as missing to the command in Sarajevo. So what you're saying, in my opinion, cannot be true because that would mean that the families did not wish to report the disappearance of their husbands, brothers, sons, fathers. This is impossible. This is something that did not occur in Bosnia-Herzegovina to any great degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If the army recorded its daily losses and they know then that a certain person was killed, why would that person then be reported as missing? Why would you be looking for him if it is known where the person was? They were in action and they were killed, would that be reported in such a case?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, of course it would be reported. The State Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners of War, Captured Persons, and Bodies of People Killed and Record of People Killed, Injured, and Missing. That is the name of the commission, and the commission's task was to take bodily remains from the enemy of all members of the army, of all civilians, and so on and so forth. So the fact that possibly the military knew about somebody's death would not prevent the commission from seeking the remains of that person to be handed over. So I'm saying that this, what you're saying, cannot be true because that would mean that the persons were not interested in the fate of their loved ones, which is impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, I would like to tender these three pages of the minutes of the B and H Presidency meeting for identification until we get a translation of those pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness said that he wasn't aware of what was going on in the Presidency, and what -- Mr. Karadzic has read into the record the relevant portions of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, that was my view, Dr. Karadzic. The relevant parts of the documents, which are the only parts that we would take notice of and want to ask questions about, are actually in the transcript and are identifiable from the questions and answers. So I don't think you need to have this exhibited.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have 1D5518 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And were you at the meeting -- earlier you said that you did not attend the meeting at which it was determined that civilians were detained in Tarcin, who should not have been there. In the minutes it states that you were present at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I was at the meeting of the Presidency that dealt with a certain item on the agenda. I didn't attend the entire meeting. The meeting would cover a number of items. I would be present only for one particular item of the agenda as a kind of rapporteur. So I do confirm that I did attend the Presidency session when the status of detainees in the Silos prison in Tarcin was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, would you agree that this is a table representing exhumations for the Srebrenica regions, ten municipalities where exhumations were carried out from 1995 to 1996. Can we look at the last page now, please, and can you look at this mass grave, common grave, and individual grave. Mass, common, and individual. Are you -- are you familiar with this table? Throughout the war, Mr. Masovic, a total of 8.831 bodies were exhumed, and you can look at the dates, the time when they were killed covering an area of ten municipalities, the entire region of Podrinje throughout the three and a half years of the war, 43 or 44 months long, meant that 1.313 bodies were exhumed from individual graves and 7.503 bodies from exhumed from mass graves. What do you say now?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: This document refers - if the title is correct - to the period from 1995 to 2006. There is no information for the last six or seven years. I don't know where this information comes from. Perhaps it comes from us at the institute since it's 2006. Most probably then this was the Federal Commission for Missing Persons, but I cannot decide -- conclude what this is about based only on the heading. Is it a list of graves? Is it a number of victims? What is this table showing?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll up so that we can see the bottom of the page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
