utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see the bottom of the page, and you can see that this is data from the Federal Commission for Missing Persons from May 2007. I assume that it was from the federal commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So at that time it was claimed that in Srebrenica alone, in July 1995, 8.000 Muslims were killed, and you can see that it was known that in the entire region and throughout the wartime period -- can we scroll down a bit to have a look at the dates of death. Could we scroll down. No, we don't have the dates of death here, but we will show you a different document that refers to those dates. So does this concern ten municipalities and regions? We can have a look at them. Zvornik, Vlasenica, Bratunac, Srebrenica. I don't know whether you included Milici or treated Milici as a separate municipality. So there are ten municipalities.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: If it's not a problem, could you go back to the first page so that we can see what this list represents? Does it only concern the victims in Srebrenica in July 1995, or does it relate to something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It concerns the victims throughout the wartime period. We'll show you another document about that, but this concerns exhumations that were conducted at the time. When was there that funeral in Tombak Mahali? From Bijeljina. It was towards the end of March, the 31st of March, 1992, and it was on the 1st of April, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know when that funeral took place but the disappearances in Bijeljina started around the 1st of April, 1992. And I assume, though this can't be seen in the table, I assume that the victims who were exhumed in Tombak Mahala were buried in 1992 or 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could this document be admitted and then I'll move on to another one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure what the witness has actually said about the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, the -- there's some reference to it, and it would assist, actually, the Chamber to have it to put the transcript into context, so we'll admit it for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2229, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it your position -- or in fact with regard to all the exhumations and mass graves, how would you say that these people died? I'm talking about mass graves in particular but also about individual graves.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't an eyewitness, but on the basis of the fact that the majority were buried in mass graves, and also given that the vast majority or the majority from those mass graves were transferred to secondary and tertiary graves, on that basis I believe that there are grounds that could lead to the conclusion that they were killed. Why would someone bury victims in mass graves? Why would bulldozers then tamper with those graves and break the bodies up, and why would these remains then be transported to other locations and buried there? Why would all this be done if these victims were not illegally killed? Why would this have been done if these things hadn't been illegal?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So that is the basis on which you made that claim. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as you know, there are eyewitnesses who survived the executions so that they witnessed, they were often present when certain victims were buried, and this is something that you know from other trial cases. There were insiders who referred to executions of tens, hundreds, or thousands of people in Kravica, Branjevo, Pilica, et cetera, and there are also satellite images that are available. So this is just some of the evidence I am aware of, and this is evidence that indicates that people -- or, rather, the remains of the people found in mass graves are the remains of people who were illegally killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please see 1D5517.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have a look at it. These are cases in which the dates of death from the Prosecution in 2005 don't correspond to the time or date of death in lists provided by the ABiH. Are you aware of the fact that these discrepancies exist? For example, in the ABiH lists the date of death is the 10th of January, 1994, and then, for example, it was changed. Have a look at number 5, for example. This doesn't need to be broadcast. It's not necessary. So it was disputed, or, rather, a correction was made and the date mentioned was the 12th of July, 1995. The place of death was said to be Buljim, and these remains were found in Glogova 2. And then we have the first two, four, five cases that aren't disputed. He was killed on the 26th of April, 1992. And then we have another one on the 26th of April, and then a third one on the 10th of January, 1994, found in Kozluk, and we go on. The six one is disputed and there was a correction made and then we have the other names. Have a look at all of this. I'll read this out. Well, no, I won't read it out. I don't know if these names should be confidential. It shouldn't be broadcast perhaps. Have a look at this. Every fifth name has been corrected. Towards the bottom there are more corrections, somewhat more corrections but the Armija has information according to which on the 15th of May, it's in the middle of the document, on the 15th of May, 1992, there was someone killed who was buried in Cancari. It was on the 17th of July, 1992, in fact, and this person was found in Cancari. And now the army has information that someone was killed on the 22nd of April, 1994, and someone made a correction and said it was on the 12th of July, 1995. How could the army expect someone who died in 1994 to be killed in 1995? And they were all found in mass graves, aren't they -- weren't they?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: This is the first time I've seen the document, and I really can't comment on it. I didn't create the document. I've never seen it before. But I'll tell you something else, in Srebrenica there are eight individuals who have the same name and surname, and they all went missing. There are two such cases in Bosnia and Herzegovina. You have eight individuals with the same first and last name. All eight of them went missing. There are four individuals -- or, rather, four cases of people who have the same name. That concerns seven individuals. There are 16 cases of people who have the same first and last name, and that concerns a group of five. 179 cases of two individuals with the same first and last name and they all disappeared. So if you want to make any comparisons - this is what I'm trying to tell you - you have to have complete information about all victims to see whether you are dealing with two different individuals or whether the person concerned is just one person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And information such as the name of the father and date of birth, does such information assist one? You have the date of birth according to Armija and the date of birth according to the OTP list. Can we see the following page. Can you see these cases where corrections were not made and we also ask on what basis were corrections made when they were made. Have a look at this. You see the name, the name of the father, the date of birth, and, well, these four items can't be identical for more than two individuals. Isn't that correct? These are all grave sites found by the ICMP. Do you doubt or do you accept that they found people in those mass graves who were killed at an earlier date? And this is something that is not disputed. Liplje, Bljeceva, Cancari 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Vlasenica, Zeleni Jadar 5. In all these graves people who had been killed earlier were found. In your opinion, was this possible? According to the information you have, in fact. Let's leave opinions aside. Opinions are problematic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Sorry, Dr. Karadzic, there are at least six questions embedded in what was, in fact, mostly a statement and you have but 15 minutes left, so what is the essence of the information that you really want from this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, what I want to find out is whether it is possible that these 260-odd, and there were those many cases in which information didn't tally, is it possible that with regard to those people that they were buried in mass graves but, in fact, it can be seen that they were killed earlier and then corrections were subsequently made, although the Armija had information on the fact that they were previously killed? So were these graves filled in with the remains of individuals who were killed at some prior time, and this is clearly illustrated by this list. The witness was a participant in a group that was involved in performing exhumations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me repeat this. I can't comment on a document that I have never seen before, a document that I did not produce myself. This document doesn't contain sufficient information to draw conclusions of any case, and this is because of what I've already said. For example, in the case of eight individuals, these individuals have fathers whose name is the same. I can provide you with this information which I have in the hotel. Their father's name is actually identical. Some of them were even born in the same year. They don't share the same dates of birth, but in certain cases you have two individuals for whom four important criteria are identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's have a look at -- let's have a look at Omerovic, Tahir, son of Zahir. Where is he recorded? Where was this person killed and in what manner? Found in Hodzici Road 5. Where was he killed? How was he killed?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: The Hodzici 5 grave was one that The Hague Tribunal exhumed. It wasn't the State Commission or the institute. Investigators from The Hague Tribunal were involved in the exhumation. All the victims in Hodzici 5 grave were victims. They went missing in Srebrenica in July 1995. In the very same grave victims from 1992 and 1995 were found, and you can find that in my table, table number 2 that has been adopted -- that has been admitted here by the Chamber, and you can see that in the grave dug in 1992 it contains the bodies of Bosniaks. You can see that in that very same grave bodies of victims from 1995 were buried. But you will see in Table 2 that we made a clear distinction between those who were victims in 1992 and those who were victims in 1995. So the victims from 1992 from Bljecevo weren't represented as victims from the year 1995. This distinction was clearly made. There were 30 remains from the Bljecevo grave, whereas there were 120 from Srebrenica in 1995. So there were 30 victims from 1992, and there were 120 victims from 1995, and that is clearly indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What sort of information do you have about clearing the battle-field? When this is done, are remains buried individually or in mass graves? Are the bodies buried in individual graves or mass graves?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I personally have no experience with clearing the terrain. In the course of the war it was impossible to go over to the enemy side. In the post-war period it was possible to do that, but this probably depends on a lot of circumstances, the time, the terrain, the identity of the victims. The manner in which taking sanitation and hygiene measures on the battle-field depends on many things. Does it concern victims of a war, of natural catastrophes, and so on and so forth? I have no information about that matter though.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this list please be admitted into evidence, Your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, at the moment I can't see a reason to oppose its admission. I mean, the witness has said that the -- I mean, he's talked about the document because Mr. Karadzic has taken him to certain entries, but he's said that he didn't produce it. He really can't talk to the document, but it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: That was my view. It seems to be another case where because of the very limited amount of information that the witness could give they -- that's contained within the transcript in any event.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That was my initial reaction, Your Honour, as I said to the last document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I think that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: And I should have asked you before, Ms. Sutherland, do you have any re-examination in respect of this --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: A minute or two?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, not very long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: So be it. Thank you. Dr. Karadzic, again, the essential information is contained within the transcript, so there's no need to readmit it. And while I think about it, the last document that we admitted, which was given the reference ID of 5518 should have been marked for identification because it wasn't translated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Excellencies, in this statement I have 118 paragraphs whereby the witness kindly said that some statements were not the topic of his interest and perhaps that will make things easier, however, I have more questions. Is Mr. Masovic able to stay for one more session tomorrow, because we will finish 084 early most probably. Well, really, it's vast material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, I understand from the witness's earlier observations that he has to be on a -- be leaving The Hague at 9.00, so the chances of finishing the other witness before then and having any meaningful time seems to me to be nil. Dr. Karadzic, the Court has done its best to accommodate you in light of the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at 1D5520, then, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, how many Serbs disappeared in Sarajevo? You confirmed, isn't that right, that Serbs did not report their missing dear ones to you until after the war, and after the war it was only a number of cases; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I did not confirm that. Some Serbian families did report their missing relatives to the State Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners of War, later the War Commission, but I agree with you that the majority of Serbs would report their missing ones during the war to colleagues in the Central Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners of War and Prisoners. According to information that I have through my work in earlier commissions and today in my work in the Institute for Missing Persons, this number, and I'm going to be precise, the precise number of missing persons of Serb ethnicity in the area of ten municipalities including --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- that number is between 350 and 380. This is not the total number of victims of Serb ethnicity in Sarajevo. This number is significantly greater. For the most part, shelling is responsible and sniper fire of the town of Sarajevo for their deaths, but there were cases when Serbs were killed in the city of Sarajevo and they were not the victims of shelling or sniper fire. A known case of that is the Ristovic family. Six members of that family were killed in Sarajevo. Their names are not on the list of the missing, because their bodies were handed over to their family and buried in the Lav cemetery. But we can say that the number of killed Serbs in Sarajevo is larger than 350 to 380, which is the figure of those reported as missing. The number perhaps according to some NGO estimates can be 450 of those who were killed and for whose death are responsible people who lived in Sarajevo, including members of some military formations. You know that there were trials organised to some of them who were accessible and who were responsible for the death of the family Ristovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If we had time it would have been very good for us to hear what you have to say, but can we look at the next page, please. What I am showing to you, Mr. Masovic, is an outdated list of Serb persons who went missing or were killed only in the part of Sarajevo that was under the control of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Army -- or, rather, the Muslims, and that list states that there were over 3.200 of such persons. The latest lists with the first and last name, the place, and the most precise data amount to 5.500 Serbs killed in Sarajevo under Muslim control. Do you have these people on your lists that we see here? We have 180 pages like this one. And you can ask for them to scroll through these pages for you. Number 2, taken to the restaurant Amerikanac in July 1992 where the command of some paramilitary formation was located. Third, missing in Sarajevo on the 1st of July 1992. Fourth, taken from her apartment at Civljane. First and last name, name of father, date of birth, year of birth. There was an old lady who was born in 1905 who was taken from her apartment. She's on this list. What would you say, Mr. Masovic, when we prove here that more than 5.500 Serbs were killed in that small part of the town which was under Muslim control?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the second page, the third page, so that the witness can look at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Karadzic, allow the witness to respond before moving on to anything else. First of all, Mr. Masovic, have you ever seen this document or have any knowledge of the contents of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am seeing this document today for the first time. I have no knowledge of the document. I cannot see who drafted it. If I were to embark on any kind of analysis, I do know a lot of things, we could go through the entire document, and I could give my comments possibly, but I don't really see any need for that because I am seeing it for the first time. The names that I'm reading, that we're scrolling through right now, do not mean anything to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Karadzic, there you have it. There's no point in going through this document with this witness, certainly not to this juncture. It would be better if you brought it into effect through a bar table motion in due course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, you talked about the exchange of civilians and that only later you agreed to civilian exchanges. So you are saying that the Serbs were offering you Muslim civilians in exchange for Serb civilians; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we must differentiate between two groups of civilians, civilians who were not in prisons and civilians who were in prisons. When we're speaking generally about civilians, there are two such groups. One group is of those who are in prison and the others who are not. My report dealt with both of these groups, and there was an attempt for people who were not in prisons to be included in the process of population exchange or, to put it more correctly, the ethnic cleansing of territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's narrow it down a little bit. Is it true that on the Bratstvo i Jedinstvo bridge there were exchanges not only of prisoners of war but also exchanges of people who were on the lists drafted by their relatives on the other side, that they would cross the line of separation for this exchange in Sarajevo, for example.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if this did take place, this was outside of the mandate of the State Commission and it did not participate in that, if these things did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, this is absolutely your last question, because regardless of anything else, we would have to rise for staff purposes. So last question to allow for some two minutes of re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would really -- perhaps we're going to have to recall this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But let me ask you this: Would the Serbs have been angry had you released 3.000 Serbs from Sarajevo, which is what Bulajic requested, without them in turn releasing Muslims? Would you have agreed to a release of the Serbs without them in turn releasing Muslims?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: You saw from my report that I absolutely refused even any thought of discussing ethnic cleansing with Mr. Bulajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you're talking about exchanges. I'm talking about the request to release people. Bulajic gave you a request -- a list of 3.000 people that he wanted released from Sarajevo. Would you have let these people go without that being part of an exchange?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is a very hypothetical question. How could I know who would think what? I did not want to take part in such dishonourable actions. I did not wish to participate in any action taking people from their houses and apartments for the purposes of relocation regardless of whether they wanted that or not. I really don't know what those people thought. I recognise one first and last name on that list of names of 3.000. Actually it wasn't me. It was my colleague Slavko Asceric, lawyer, who was at the time the head of the exchange commission and deputy police minister of Republika Srpska. When he saw his name and the name of his wife as persons who were being sought by the other side, by Serbs who were asking for him to be allowed to leave Sarajevo, he laughed. He pointed out his name and the name of his wife, and then after that I gave the list to Mr. Bulajic and I spoke those words: Colleague Bulajic, I do not need a telephone directory of the Serbs in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, I'm afraid we have run out --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he didn't answer my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, I think he did in his own way and we must leave it at that. Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, just in the last couple of answers that you gave to Mr. Karadzic and you talked about, you know, this was referred to "in my report" about the exchanging of civilians and the reference to -- that you made about ethnic cleansing, you were in fact referring to your amalgamated witness statement, were you not? When you were talking about in your report, you actually meant your amalgamated witness statement where you discuss in some detail about the exchanging and the pressure you were put under by the Bosnian Serbs to exchange civilians; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Earlier on today Mr. Karadzic, this is at page 75 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: We have maximum of two minutes before the tape runs out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: He said that he unilaterally released about 4.000 individuals from Manjaca so that they could be taken to other countries and then you said that you were surprised by that because you -- you know that a number went to Manjaca, and that then, in fact, on page 76 he said that -- you said that you thought that the ICRC even launched a protest with the Serbian authorities if you remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter number 13031 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, this is 11031. I don't think it's the correct document and I'm sorry if I misspoke. It's a communication to the press number 92 of 36, dated the 16th of December, 1992, from ICRC, and you see in the second paragraph it there says it's been suggested -- talking about the release of the prisoners from Manjaca and then the ICRC has actually requested information about 529 detainees transferred from Manjaca camp without its delegates' knowledge and whose whereabouts remain unknown. Is that what you were referring to in your answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: The witness is nodding, for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. That is the public ICRC protest, because of the concealment of 529 -- I did say 500 detainees. It's not a protest, it's a request.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and if I can just refer Your Honours, as I don't have time to take the witness to the document, to Exhibit P03727 which is an official note filed at the Batkovic camp receiving 532 prisoners from Manjaca camp on the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, the witness couldn't speak to that document anyway --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- 13th of December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: -- unless he was aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: We have now really run --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: -- completely out of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And I tender that document I just showed the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: So be it. Mr. Masovic, thank you very much for attending the Tribunal. Your evidence is now concluded. Have a safe journey back home. We will all rise together, and we'll meet again tomorrow morning at 8.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 11th day of April, 2012, at 8.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.28 p.m.,
